readings.title: 6 ways to give that aren’t about money
body: Good news: You can be a generous person without writing a bunch of checks. In fact, many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need. This type of giving is open to everyone.
Many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need.

Not sure where to begin? Here are six gifts of time and attention that have the strong potential to spark ripple effects that affect millions, from head of TED Chris Anderson’s new book, Infectious Generosity .

Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh taught that attention is the most precious gift we can give someone. This is where generosity starts — with a willingness to stop focusing on ourselves and to instead pay attention to someone else and their needs. From that act of connection, anything can happen.

Truth is, it can be difficult. We spend much of our time lost in our own worlds. We are often reluctant to focus on the issues that others are dealing with. So we put up shields. And that means that many of the people who could really use our attention never feel seen by us. The generosity of attention is therefore the generosity of being willing to be a little uncomfortable, to take down those shields, to give up some time, to risk coming to care about someone else.
Whether you stop and have a meaningful connection with a person in need or spend 30 minutes researching a cause you think might matter, you have already begun your generosity journey.

In our connected era, there’s a type of generosity that matters more than ever: a willingness to reach out to those with whom we disagree with. Many disputes today play out in public online. Huge audiences can become glued to online feuds. What if we could bring a satisfying resolution to more of these conflicts?

It’s hard to reach out to our critics. This is a particularly challenging form of the generosity mindset. You are sacrificing your personal comfort for the greater good of bringing people together. But if you’re successful, there’s a powerful knock-on benefit: You are helping change the tone of public discussion today. That’s a gift to all of us.
The single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.
In countless circumstances, the single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.

Our single biggest piece of advice to someone coming to speak on the TED stage is to think of their talk not as an opportunity to pitch something (like a business or a cause) but rather as a gift. It is a chance to freely share valuable ideas with the audience. And those ideas have the potential to impact a listener’s life for years to come.

If you possess knowledge that others may benefit from, consider how you could share it to create ripple effects. What may take you a few hours to prepare and act on could light up someone’s life — and that could just be the beginning.

In our connected age, the networks we have access to matter more than ever. Therefore, one of the most important forms of viral generosity is to help people connect with others. The simplest way to do this is to make an introduction.

As psychologist and TED speaker Adam Grant has argued, an introduction can be fairly easy to give — and unbelievably valuable to receive. Ask many people how they met their partner, got their dream job or found the perfect collaborator for their creative project, and the answer will often be the same: someone — a friend, a neighbor, a colleague — introduced them to the right person. What you’re effectively doing is giving someone else access to your network of resources. And those introductions can have exponential consequences.

In his remarkable book Human Universals , anthropologist Donald Brown documented how hospitality is one of hundreds of human behaviors that have been observed in every single culture ever studied. But if hospitality is so ubiquitous (and so pleasant), is it really a form of generosity? Well, yes. Quite apart from any costs involved, it takes effort to invite someone over, whether friends or possible future friends. It’s easier just to watch the next episode of the TV series you’re into.
So how can hospitality contribute to infectious generosity? Hospitality taps into our deepest instincts for connection to one another. And each experience of it evokes a desire to reciprocate.
People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment.

Pioneering artist Lily Yeh was approached by the dancer and choreographer Arthur L. Hall to undertake a community art project in a derelict, abandoned plot in her home city of Philadelphia. “I was interested but totally scared,” Yeh recalled. “I had little resources and no experience in working outdoors in a community setting. I wanted to run away, but I did not want to see a coward in the mirror. So I stepped into the project.”

The community project became the Village of Arts and Humanities, an art park full of trees, sculptures and mosaics created by local adults and children in collaboration with Yeh. Yeh’s work led her to a profound realization: that creating beauty in public spaces is profoundly healing and transformative for communities.

People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment. Those who can enchant can offer a gift of immense value.

6种不花钱的给予方式
2024年1月22日
/
克里斯·安德森
Facebook
X
LinkedIn
Reddit
WhatsApp
MINIWIDE / iStock
好消息：你不必写下一堆支票，也能成为一个慷慨的人。事实上，许多最令人敬畏且最有效的慷慨之举，都是量身定制、针对特定需求的时间与精力、才华与爱的馈赠。这种给予方式对每个人开放。

##段落
许多最令人敬畏且最有效的慷慨之举，都是量身定制、针对特定需求的时间与精力、才华与爱的馈赠。
不知道从何开始？以下是六种时间与关注力的馈赠，它们有巨大潜力引发波及数百万人的涟漪效应，摘自TED掌门人克里斯·安德森的新书《传染性慷慨》。

##段落
1. 转移关注
禅宗大师一行禅师教导说，关注是我们能给予他人最珍贵的礼物。慷慨由此开始——愿意停止关注自我，转而关注他人及其需求。从这种联结的行为出发，一切皆有可能。

##段落
事实上，这并不容易。我们大部分时间都迷失在自己的世界里。我们常常不愿去关注他人正在面对的问题。于是我们竖起盾牌。这意味着许多真正需要我们关注的人，从未感受到被我们看见。因此，关注的慷慨，就是愿意让自己稍感不适、卸下那些盾牌、牺牲一些时间、冒险去在意他人的慷慨。

##段落
无论你是停下来与需要帮助的人建立一次有意义的联结，还是花30分钟研究一个你认为可能重要的议题，你都已经踏上了慷慨之旅。

##段落
2. 搭建桥梁
在我们这个互联的时代，有一种慷慨比以往任何时候都更重要：愿意主动接触那些与我们意见相左的人。如今许多争端都在线上公开上演。大量观众可能会被网络论战牢牢吸引。如果我们能为更多这样的冲突带来令人满意的解决，会怎样？

##段落
主动接触批评者很难。这是慷慨心态中极具挑战性的一种形式。你是在为了促进人们团结这一更大的善，而牺牲自己的个人舒适。但如果你成功了，会有一个强大的附带好处：你在帮助改变当今公共讨论的基调。这是给所有人的礼物。

##段落
我们能给予的最大礼物是知识——能解决问题、满足需求或开辟前进道路的知识。

##段落
3. 分享知识
在无数情境中，我们能给予的最大礼物是知识——能解决问题、满足需求或开辟前进道路的知识。
我们对某人的最大建议是……

在TED舞台上发言，最关键的思考方式不是将演讲视为推销某样东西（比如一个项目或一项事业）的机会，而是将其视为一份礼物。这是一个与听众自由分享宝贵想法的契机，而这些想法有可能在未来数年影响一位听众的生活。

如果你拥有他人可能受益的知识，请思考如何分享它，以产生涟漪效应。你花几个小时准备和行动的内容，可能会点亮某个人的生活——而这可能仅仅是个开始。

4. 促成连接

在这个互联的时代，我们所能触及的网络比以往任何时候都重要。因此，病毒式慷慨最重要的形式之一，就是帮助人们与他人建立联系。最简便的方式就是引荐。

正如心理学家及TED演讲者亚当·格兰特所言，引荐对给予者来说相当容易——而对接受者而言却价值非凡。问问许多人他们是如何遇见伴侣、获得梦想工作或找到创意项目的完美合作者的，答案往往相同：有人——朋友、邻居或同事——将他们引荐给了合适的人。你实际上是在为他人打开通往你资源网络的大门，而这些引荐可能带来指数级的连锁效应。

5. 展现好客

在人类学家唐纳德·布朗的杰出著作《人类共性》中，他记录了待客之道是如何成为在所有被研究文化中都能观察到的数百种人类行为之一。但既然好客如此普遍（且如此愉悦），它真的算是一种慷慨吗？嗯，是的。撇开任何成本不谈，邀请某人来访需要付出努力，无论是朋友还是潜在的未来朋友。只顾着追下一集你正沉迷的电视剧肯定更容易。

那么，好客如何促进病毒式慷慨呢？好客触及我们与他人连接的最深层本能，而每一次好客体验都会唤起回报的渴望。

人们当然需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健，但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑和超越——这些正是魅力的所有元素。

6. 创造魅力

先锋艺术家莉莉·叶被舞蹈家兼编舞家亚瑟·L·霍尔邀请，在她家乡费城一块废弃荒芜的地块上开展社区艺术项目。“我感兴趣但完全害怕，”叶回忆道。“我资源匮乏，也没有在社区环境中户外工作的经验。我想逃跑，但我不想在镜子里看到懦夫。所以我走进了这个项目。”

这个社区项目后来成为“艺术与人文之村”，一个充满树木、雕塑和马赛克的艺术公园，由当地成年人

与叶合作的成人和儿童。叶的工作让她有了深刻的领悟：在公共空间中创造美，对社区而言具有深远的疗愈和变革力量。
人们当然需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑和超越——这些都是“迷人”的元素。能够带来迷人体验的人，能赠予一份无比珍贵的礼物。

readings.title: The overlooked benefits of laughing at yourself
body: 15 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Laurie Clarke Research shows it's sometimes good for us to poke fun at ourselves, but not always. Here's how to harness the benefits, while avoiding the pitfalls. Why do some schoolchildren become outcasts? In the 1990s, psychologists set out to investigate why some kids were excluded by their peers. They discovered two archetypes. Some of the rejected children were bullying and aggressive. Others were meek and subservient. Both shared one quality: an inability to take a joke .  The first group was responded to teasing with anger or violence, while the second felt wounded and withdrew. Both interpreted the intended humour as an insult, something that couldn't possibly be in good faith. More socially assured kids, on the other hand, shrugged off teasing, or were amused by it. Whether we can laugh at ourselves can clearly have consequences from an early age.  Studies show that throughout life, a more light-hearted and humorous outlook on life is better for your mental health, relationships and overall prospects. Still, opinion on whether it is a good idea to laugh at yourself specifically has long been divided. Now, though, researchers are finally beginning to understand the nuance of what it really means to poke fun at ourselves – and when and how it might be beneficial. Is it even possible to laugh at yourself? Plato didn't think so. The Ancient Greek philosopher believed that humour was triggered by feeling superior to others – particularly those who delusionally believe they are better-looking or wiser than they really are. If you really hate people laughing at you, you could be a gelotophobe – someone with an acute sensitivity to laughter More than 1,000 years later, in 1651, English philosopher Thomas Hobbes largely agreed . The exception – when people were occasionally able to laugh at themselves – was when reflecting on a past foolishness, which demonstrated how much worldlier they had become in the interim. Eventually, philosophers began to allow that not all humour was motivated by spite. In the 18th Century, for example, the popular "incongruity theory" proposed that hilarity often results from an unexpected violation of social norms. Still, whether people can actually laugh at themselves remained a contentious topic right up until recent times. Most humour research from the past 50 years has relied on asking people if they can laugh at themselves and taking their word for it. But like the weekly units of alcohol people confess to on doctors' forms, there was a possibility that the reports were a little aspirational. Perhaps people weren't quite as sporting as they claimed. In 2011, though, European researchers tested the ability using an experimental set-up instead. They invited test subjects into the lab and covertly videotaped their faces. When they next came in, the subjects were presented with distorted, fun-house mirror style images of their faces, and their reactions were recorded. Not everyone was amused, but 80% at least smiled when unexpectedly encountering the image. Forty per cent were extra tickled and laughed aloud. "Now the science is quite settled that yes, it is possible to laugh at oneself, and there are actually quite numerous benefits associated with that," says Sonja Heintz, a lecturer in psychology at Plymouth University, UK, who researches humour. Being able to laugh at yourself is one of the most challenging types of humour to master, claimed influential American humour researcher Paul McGhee in 2010. In McGhee's seven-step humour programme (targeted at those suffering "terminal seriousness" like Plato), learning to laugh at oneself was the penultimate step – second only in difficulty to "finding humour in stressful situations."  McGhee saw laughing at yourself as the gateway to other types of humour; a "core component" of a more mirthful existence. "Because if someone takes themselves very seriously, it's difficult to engage in humour in general," explains Heintz.   Some find self-mockery easier to master than others. If you really hate people laughing at you, you could be a gelotophobe – someone with an acute sensitivity to laughter. "You might be sitting in a cafe and joking with your friends, and someone might approach you and ask, why did you laugh at me?" says René Proyer, psychology professor at Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg in Germany. For gelotophobes, even a smile can indicate their interlocutor thinks them a ridiculous person.  There is no one factor explaining why one might become a gelotophobe, but Proyer says that a very strict and punishing style of parenting is one risk factor . Another is an early traumatic experience of having been laughed at. "So a really embarrassing situation at school, for example," says Proyer, "where you are the butt of jokes for weeks, months, perhaps years." Autism appears to be another risk factor . There also seems to be a cultural dimension. East Asian countries generally have higher levels of gelotophobia than Western nations, something researchers attribute to those belonging to collectivistic cultures being less likely to single themselves out for attention, or to engage in humour as a coping mechanism. These cultures tend to believe humour is best left to the professionals. In China, for example, people are more likely to associate humour with "experts", i.e. comedians, than everyday citizens. Like the children unable to take teasing, gelotophobes tend to experience worse psychological and interpersonal outcomes. The trait has been tied to lower life satisfaction, greater friendship avoidance, and increased loneliness and depression. The opposite trait is gelotophilia, the joy of being laughed at by others, which has been linked to stronger social connectedness. One way this can manifest is in "playfulness", the tendency to take oneself and the world lightly. "Playful people are able to frame or reframe everyday situations in a way such that they experience them as entertaining or intellectually stimulating or personally interesting," says Proyer. "A highly playful person is able to do a boring task or chore and reframe it in a way that is somewhat amusing." Research has established playfulness as a predictor of higher self-esteem and relationship satisfaction .  Most experts agree that humour is beneficial to our relationships. But the kind of humour matters too.  In 2003, Canadian researchers developed the Humor Styles Questionnaire , which divides people's dominant humour type into four categories: affiliative humour, self-enhancing humour, aggressive humour and self-defeating humour.  The questionnaire soon became hugely influential. "It was the first time anyone had considered that humour could be adaptive but also maladaptive," says Claire Fox, professor of psychology of education at the University of Bristol, UK.  Self-enhancing humourists are attuned to the fragile absurdities of humanity and existence. They agree with statements like: "If I am feeling upset or unhappy I usually try to think of something funny about the situation to make myself feel better". These individuals make light of their problems as a coping mechanism. This was seen as an adaptive humour type. "Self-defeating" humour, on the other hand, was thought to be maladaptive. Self-defeating humourists agree with statements like: "I often try to make people like or accept me more by saying something funny about my own weaknesses, blunders, or faults." At the time, this type of humour was seen as signalling neediness and low self-esteem. When Heintz first began researching humour in the 2010s, she was taken aback to find that poking fun at oneself was viewed so negatively by the field. "Because my personal humour style is [that] I make fun of myself all the time," she says. "I don't take myself seriously." Reading the literature, Heintz was surprised to find that someone like her was supposedly at higher risk of anxiety, depression and suicidal ideation. To find out if self-defeatists really were all that self-loathing, Heintz rounded up a group of them and compared them to those with other humour styles. If the predominant thinking was correct, "these people should really suffer with mental health issues", says Heintz. But not a single one did. On the contrary, she found that self-defeating humour was associated with higher levels of self-esteem and better interpersonal relationships. "They all said, 'Well, I struggle a bit with self-esteem. I'm a bit insecure. But making fun of myself is actually a really good way for me to cope with these difficulties, and it gives me a way to connect with others'," says Heintz. Most research finding a connection between self-defeating humour and worse mental health and relationship outcomes is correlational , says Heintz, rather than showing a causal effect. Other research has found that the impacts of self-defeating humour can vary across different contexts. A 2014 study by Fox found that schoolchildren who were the victim of bullying used more self-defeating humour than others, and that this preference became more pronounced over time.  But a follow-up study she carried out in 2016 added nuance to the picture. This study labelled kids based on the type of humour they preferred. One group, dubbed the "self-defeaters", engaged only in self-defeating humour. This group seemed to fare worst, ranking the lowest for self-esteem and becoming lonelier over time. But some kids used self-defeating humour even more than the self-defeatists and didn't suffer the same ill effects. The difference was that these kids, dubbed "humour endorsers", engaged in all four different humour types. While those who solely relied on self-defeating humour suffered a social penalty, the humour endorsers did not.  "This suggested that it's actually okay to use self-defeating humour, as long as you're using it in combination with other styles of humour as well," says Fox.  It's not that self-defeating humour never poses an issue. "If you make fun of yourself and it comes from a place of bitterness and self-hatred, then yes, it's probably not good for you," says Heintz. But Heintz now believes that a lot of the negative press around self-defeating humour might  stem from a methodological issue with the Humor Styles Questionnaire. The questions relating to self-defeating humour often introduce a value judgement, she notes, specifying things like: "I do it too much. I do it more than I should."  Could this negative self-judgement be skewing the results? Heintz is now working on a forthcoming paper evaluating 25 years of the questionnaire where she'll propose a rethink of the self-defeating scale. Other researchers are already devising new scales which distinguish between truly self-defeating humour and its more adaptive varieties (like that old British standby, self-deprecating humour). As good comedians know, you should only mock yourself if you've made peace with the flaw or mistake you're making fun of. If you're making a joke from a place of discomfort, people pick up on that and feel awkward, says Heintz. "We need to know that when people make a joke, it's not to be taken seriously. That safety needs to be there for someone to respond to that humour." Moderation is also something to keep in mind. Between self-deprecating and self-defeating humour, "the distinction appears to be about excess and going overboard", says Fox.  Still, it's clear that learning to laugh at yourself can afford psychological and social benefits. Not taking yourself too seriously has been found to help with coping with life's setbacks. Part of this is the simple reason that if you make a mistake, as everyone does from time to time, you're opting for a positive emotional response (laughter) over a negative one (anger or gloom).  "It's related to self-transcendence, which means that when something goes wrong, we can keep that distance from the event and see it a bit more objectively… see the lighter side of things," says Heintz. "We also know that there is a causal effect between things like life satisfaction , coping skills and general well-being." On the interpersonal side, laughing at yourself can be an important tool in your social arsenal. "It's a very safe way to engage in humour in new situations, if you are with strangers and don't quite know their sense of humour yet," says Heintz. When there is a power differential, it can be especially expedient. Another study by Fox found that lecturers engaging in so-called self-defeating humour were seen more positively by students. And those who laugh off minor errors – as long as they do not impact others – are seen as warmer and more competent .    humour So, if you're one of the terminally serious, how can you go about cultivating a lighter attitude towards yourself? McGhee advocated zeroing in on your sore spots – whether it's your height, weight, baldness or clumsiness – and confronting these "no-laugh zones" head-on. However excruciating at first, he promised "a sense of exhilaration and liberation" will follow "as you become comfortable with joking about the things that used to simply annoy or embarrass you."  The first step is admitting to the things you don't like about yourself to others, starting with the most minor. Then start making jokes. "Let's say you're not very interested in fashion, you could poke fun at, 'Oh, I'm wearing the same old jeans again'," says Heintz. "Or, look, I did my shopping at Temu." Eventually, you're ready to make gags about your most agonising insecurities. More like this •  Why performing stand-up is good for your health •  Why do we laugh inappropriately? •  How I changed my personality in six weeks If prodding at your sore spots feels like too much, you could start by cultivating a more amused attitude in general. Proyer carried out a study where he tested whether it was possible to increase playfulness in participants using simple activities over the course of a week. For example, setting aside 10 minutes each evening to write down the three most playful things that happened during the day, "whether this was a thought that you had, or something you observed on your way to work", says Proyer. By and large, the participants perceived themselves as more playful up to three months afterwards – as well as reporting reduced levels of depressiveness and greater happiness.  So what was the most playful thing that happened to you today? Write it down and laugh yourself silly. --  For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.  For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram .  Psychology Mental health Wellbeing Health Comedy Features

##段落

15小时前 分享 保存 设为谷歌偏好 Laurie Clarke 研究表明，自嘲有时对我们有益，但并非总是如此。以下是如何利用其好处，同时避免陷阱。

##段落

为什么有些学童会成为被排斥者？20世纪90年代，心理学家着手调查为什么有些孩子被同龄人排挤。他们发现了两种原型。一些被排斥的孩子欺凌好斗。另一些则温顺服从。两者共有一个特质：无法接受玩笑。第一组对戏弄的反应是愤怒或暴力，而第二组感到受伤并退缩。两者都将本意幽默的言辞解读为侮辱，认为那不可能出于善意。相比之下，社交更自信的孩子对戏弄不以为意，或觉得有趣。我们能否自嘲，显然从幼年起就会产生后果。

##段落

研究表明，纵观一生，对生活持更轻松幽默的态度，更有利于心理健康、人际关系和整体前景。尽管如此，关于自嘲本身是否可取，长期以来意见不一。但现在，研究人员终于开始理解自嘲的真正含义及其何时何地可能有益的细微差别。

##段落

自嘲甚至可能吗？柏拉图不这么认为。这位古希腊哲学家相信，幽默源于对他人的优越感——尤其是那些自欺欺人地认为自己比实际更漂亮或更聪明的人。如果你真的讨厌别人嘲笑你，你可能是个“被笑恐惧症”患者——对笑声极度敏感的人。

##段落

一千多年后的1651年，英国哲学家托马斯·霍布斯大体上同意这一观点。例外情况——人们偶尔能自嘲——是在反思过去的愚蠢行为时，这证明了他们在此期间变得多么老练世故。最终，哲学家们开始承认并非所有幽默都出于恶意。例如，在18世纪，流行的“不协调理论”提出，狂笑往往源于对社会规范的意外违背。尽管如此，直到近代，人们是否真的能自嘲仍是一个有争议的话题。

##段落

过去50年的大部分幽默研究依赖于询问人们是否能自嘲，并相信他们的话。但就像人们在医生表格上坦白的每周酒精摄入量一样，这些报告有可能有点理想化。也许人们并不像他们声称的那样大度。然而在2011年，欧洲研究人员改用实验设置来测试这种能力。他们邀请了测试对象……

他们将受试者带入实验室，偷偷录下他们的面部反应。当他们再次进入时，受试者被展示出扭曲的哈哈镜风格面部图像，并记录他们的反应。并非所有人都觉得有趣，但80%的人在意外看到图像时至少会微笑。40%的人格外被逗乐，放声大笑。英国普利茅斯大学心理学讲师索尼娅·海因茨研究幽默，她说：“现在科学已相当确定，是的，人能够自嘲，而且这确实带来许多益处。”2010年，有影响力的美国幽默研究者保罗·麦吉声称，能够自嘲是最难掌握的幽默类型之一。在麦吉的七步幽默计划中（针对像柏拉图那样患有“终极严肃”的人），学会自嘲是倒数第二步——难度仅次于“在压力情境中寻找幽默”。麦吉将自嘲视为通往其他幽默类型的门户，是更愉快生活的“核心组成部分”。海因茨解释说：“因为如果某人过于严肃看待自己，总体上就很难参与幽默。”有些人比其他人更容易掌握自嘲。如果你真的讨厌别人嘲笑你，你可能是“被笑恐惧症”患者——对笑声极度敏感。德国哈勒-维滕贝格大学心理学教授勒内·普罗耶说：“你可能坐在咖啡馆和朋友开玩笑，有人走近你问，你为什么嘲笑我？”对于被笑恐惧症患者，即使一个微笑也可能表明对话者认为他们可笑。没有单一因素能解释为何某人会成为被笑恐惧症患者，但普罗耶表示，非常严格且惩罚性的教养方式是一个风险因素。另一个因素是早期被嘲笑的创伤经历。普罗耶说：“比如在学校里一个非常尴尬的情况，你成为玩笑的对象，持续几周、几个月，甚至几年。”自闭症似乎是另一个风险因素。似乎也存在文化维度。东亚国家的被笑恐惧症水平普遍高于西方国家，研究人员将此归因于集体主义文化中的人不太可能单独引起注意，或不太可能将幽默作为应对机制。这些文化倾向于认为幽默最好留给专业人士。例如，在中国，人们更可能将幽默与“专家”，即喜剧演员，而非普通公民联系起来。就像无法忍受戏弄的孩子一样，被笑恐惧症患者往往经历更差的心理和人际关系结果。这种特质与较低的生活满意度有关。

满意度更高、友谊回避更少，以及孤独感和抑郁情绪的增加。相反的特质是“被笑愉悦”（gelotophilia），即享受被别人取笑的乐趣，这与更强的社会联系有关。这种特质的一种表现形式是“玩心”（playfulness），即倾向于以轻松的态度对待自己和世界。“爱玩的人能够以某种方式构建或重新构建日常情境，使其体验为有趣、激发智力或引起个人兴趣，”普罗耶尔说。“高度爱玩的人能够将无聊的任务或杂事重新构建为某种有趣的事情。”研究已将玩心确定为更高自尊和关系满意度的预测因素。

大多数专家同意，幽默对我们的人际关系有益。但幽默的种类也很重要。2003年，加拿大研究人员开发了“幽默风格问卷”，将人们的主导幽默类型分为四类：亲和型幽默、自我增强型幽默、攻击型幽默和自我挫败型幽默。该问卷迅速产生了巨大影响。“这是第一次有人考虑到幽默既可以是适应性的，也可能是适应不良的，”英国布里斯托大学教育心理学教授克莱尔·福克斯说。自我增强型幽默者善于察觉人类和存在中脆弱的荒谬之处。他们认同诸如“如果我感到心烦或不开心，我通常会试着想一些有趣的事情来让自己感觉更好”之类的说法。这些人以轻描淡写的方式应对问题，将其作为一种应对机制。这被视为一种适应性幽默类型。另一方面，“自我挫败型”幽默被认为是适应不良的。自我挫败型幽默者认同诸如“我经常试图通过说一些关于自己弱点、失误或缺陷的趣事来让别人更喜欢或接受我”之类的说法。当时，这种幽默类型被视为表明依赖性和低自尊。

当海因茨在2010年代开始研究幽默时，她惊讶地发现，拿自己开玩笑在该领域被视为如此负面的行为。“因为我的个人幽默风格就是总是拿自己开玩笑，”她说。“我不把自己太当回事。”阅读文献后，海因茨惊讶地发现，像她这样的人据称患焦虑、抑郁和自杀意念的风险更高。为了弄清楚自我挫败者是否真的如此自我厌恶，海因茨召集了一组这样的人，并将他们与其他幽默风格的人进行比较。如果主流观点是正确的，“这些人应该真的遭受心理健康问题，”海因茨说。但没有一个人如此。相反，她发现自我挫败型幽默与更高的...

较高的自尊水平和更好的人际关系。“他们都说，‘嗯，我在自尊方面有些挣扎，我有点缺乏安全感。但自嘲实际上是我应对这些困难的一个很好的方式，也给了我与他人建立联系的途径，’”海因茨说。海因茨指出，大多数发现自嘲式幽默与较差的心理健康和人际关系结果之间存在关联的研究，都是相关性研究，而非显示因果关系。其他研究发现，自嘲式幽默的影响可能因不同情境而异。福克斯在2014年进行的一项研究发现，遭受欺凌的学童比其他人更多使用自嘲式幽默，且这种偏好随时间推移变得更加明显。但她在2016年进行的后续研究为这一图景增添了细微差别。该研究根据孩子们偏好的幽默类型对他们进行分类。一个被称为“自嘲者”的群体只使用自嘲式幽默。这个群体似乎表现最差，自尊排名最低，且随着时间的推移变得更加孤独。但有些孩子使用自嘲式幽默的频率甚至高于“自嘲者”，却没有遭受同样的不良影响。区别在于，这些被称为“幽默支持者”的孩子，会使用所有四种不同的幽默类型。虽然那些仅依赖自嘲式幽默的孩子在社交上付出代价，但幽默支持者却没有。“这表明，只要你将自嘲式幽默与其他风格的幽默结合使用，它实际上是可以的，”福克斯说。这并不是说自嘲式幽默从来不会造成问题。“如果你自嘲，且这种自嘲源于痛苦和自恨，那么是的，它可能对你不利，”海因茨说。但海因茨现在认为，围绕自嘲式幽默的大量负面评价可能源于幽默风格问卷的方法论问题。她指出，与自嘲式幽默相关的问题常常引入价值判断，例如指定“我做得太多了，我做得比应该的多。”这种负面的自我判断是否会扭曲结果？海因茨目前正在撰写一篇即将发表的论文，评估该问卷25年来的使用情况，她将在其中提议重新思考自嘲量表。其他研究人员已经在设计新量表，以区分真正自嘲式幽默与其更具适应性的变体（如英国传统的自贬式幽默）。正如优秀的喜剧演员所知，只有当你对自己开玩笑的缺陷或错误已经释怀时，才应自嘲。海因茨说，如果你在不舒服的状态下开玩笑，人们会察觉到并感到尴尬。“我们需要知道，当人们开玩笑时，它不是……”

要认真对待。这种安全感必须存在，人们才会对那种幽默产生回应。”适度也是需要牢记的一点。福克斯表示，在自嘲式和自毁式幽默之间，“区别似乎在于过度和过分”。尽管如此，显然学会自嘲能带来心理和社交上的益处。研究发现，不过于把自己当回事有助于应对生活中的挫折。部分原因很简单：如果你犯了错误——每个人都会时不时犯错——你选择的是积极的情绪反应（笑声）而非消极的（愤怒或沮丧）。海因茨说：“这与自我超越有关，意味着当事情出错时，我们能保持与事件的距离，更客观地看待它……看到事物轻松的一面。”“我们还知道，生活满意度、应对技巧和整体幸福感之间存在因果关系。”在人际交往方面，自嘲可以成为你社交武器库中的重要工具。海因茨说：“在新环境中，如果与陌生人在一起，还不了解他们的幽默感，自嘲是一种非常安全的幽默方式。”当存在权力差异时，这尤其有利。福克斯的另一项研究发现，使用所谓自毁式幽默的讲师在学生眼中更受好评。而那些能一笑置之小错误的人——只要不影响他人——被视为更温暖、更能干。

幽默 所以，如果你是那种极度严肃的人，该如何培养对自己更轻松的态度呢？麦吉提倡聚焦你的痛处——无论是身高、体重、秃头还是笨拙——并直面这些“禁区”。他承诺，尽管起初可能痛苦不堪，但“随着你习惯于拿那些曾经只会让你烦恼或尴尬的事情开玩笑，一种兴奋和解放的感觉”会随之而来。第一步是向他人承认你不喜欢自己的地方，从最轻微的入手。然后开始开玩笑。海因茨说：“假设你对时尚不太感兴趣，你可以打趣说，‘哦，我又穿这条旧牛仔裤了’。”“或者，看，我在Temu上买的东西。”最终，你准备好拿自己最痛苦的不安全感来制造笑料。更多相关内容 • 为什么表演脱口秀对你的健康有益 • 我们为什么会不合时宜地笑 • 我如何在六周内改变了自己的性格 如果戳自己的痛处感觉太过分，你可以从培养总体上更愉悦的态度开始。普罗耶进行了一项研究，测试是否可能通过简单的活动增加参与者的玩乐性。

在过去一周的时间里。例如，每天傍晚留出10分钟，写下当天发生的三件最有趣的事情，“无论是你脑海中闪现的一个念头，还是上班路上观察到的某个细节”，普罗耶尔说。总体而言，参与者在之后长达三个月的时间里感觉自己更具玩心——同时报告称抑郁感降低，幸福感提升。那么，今天发生在你身上最有趣的事情是什么？把它写下来，尽情大笑一番吧。——如需获取关于健康与福祉的可靠见解，欢迎订阅由资深健康记者梅丽莎·霍根布姆撰写的《健康修复》新闻通讯，她还开设了《长寿生活》和《平静六步法》课程。欲了解更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境与健康新闻，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。心理学 心理健康 福祉 健康 喜剧 专题

readings.title: Is Italy the new tax haven for the global rich?
body: 22 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Italy has already been attacked by the French Government for using tax incentives to lure wealthy French and other international residents away, but with the war in the Middle East hurting the Gulf states, Italy has become an even more attractive location for the rich. Tax wasn't the main reason for leaving France, Robert insists over a café crème at Charles de Gaulle airport. It was the beauty of Italy, the bella vita  (the beautiful/good life), the art and the music. But for the Frenchman, buying a house in Rome and becoming an Italian tax resident was a very nice part of the package offered by the country, where high net worth individuals can pay a fixed annual tax on all foreign income – regardless of amount – and enjoy a series of other exemptions.  Robert, who describes himself as only "moderately wealthy", moved to Italy eight years ago after a career in computers which ended with him selling his company. Robert, not his real name, may not be among the French billionaires who have fled the French taxman for Italy, but the advantages to him are clear.   If he'd been buying a house in France, he would have had to pay what the French call frais de notaire (solicitor's fees) most of which goes to the government (much like Stamp Duty in the UK or Real Estate Transfer Taxes in the US). In Italy there's an exemption for the prima casa , the first house you buy. In France, President Macron transformed France's Impot sur la Fortune  (wealth tax) into an Impot sur la Fortune Immobilière  (real estate wealth tax) so stock market investments, for example, are no longer affected but "if you have ten million dollars' worth of property, this tax is very painful indeed," says Robert. Again, there's nothing like that in Italy.  In France you also have to pay a property tax ( taxe foncière or land tax). "We don't have that here for the prima casa (first home)," says Robert, although he notes "there is a high charge for refuse collection". The best thing as far as he is concerned is that there is no inheritance tax on property you own in Italy up to €1 million ($1.1 million) and it's only 4% beyond that threshold. In France the tax-free limit is much lower – €100,000 ($110,000) – and beyond that it's a sliding scale up to a top rate of 45%. But it's for the seriously rich that Italy starts to look like a fiscal paradise. "I have friends who have moved here for tax reasons and others who are thinking about it," Robert tells me. "For people who really pay a lot of tax, Italy is very attractive because of it's "flat tax". In Italy, the taxman fixes an upper limit of tax that can be levied on income. However much you earn, you never pay more than that. The upper limit is now €300,000 ($353,000). Although not long ago it was €100,000 before rising to €200,000. If you're paying a million euros of income tax a year in France, Italy is very tempting. As for US citizens, Americans are always taxable on worldwide income, so moving to Italy would not help their tax bill. Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe – Peter Ferrigno Robert tells me that he has two rich French friends who have moved to Italy in the past few months, but they came from the UK. They were both working in finance in the City of London and were keen to move to a place where the fiscal regime was as sympathetic to them as the one Britain had before it changed the rules for wealthy foreign residents.  "Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe. And it means you get tax certainty and clarity, within the heart of Europe, rather than having to go a long way," says Peter Ferrigno, director of tax services at wealth migration specialists Henley & Partners. "We have meetings with people every week who would like to leave France," says Paris-based tax lawyer Jerome Barre. "They are unhappy about the tax situation now and they are worried that it will become harsher in the future. People are not confident with the political climate. Taxes are changing a lot, almost every year. People are frightened that after the election of the new president in 2027, things could become harder than today," he says. At this stage though it's more "questions from entrepreneurs and wealthy people who are wondering if they would like to move or not move rather than people actually moving," Jerome Barre explains. "Relocation requires full commitment and careful structuring," he stresses. He adds that for business-owners  " they need to change the seat of the company. They are subject in France to an exit tax." If many wealthy French people are at the "thinking-about-moving" stage, the question is being felt even more acutely in the United Arab Emirates. It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE – Peter Ferrigno But giving up on Dubai's zero-tax regime will be very difficult for many. "When you are in a country where you do not pay any tax, it's very difficult to come back to a country where you have to pay a lot. Especially for those used to spending a lot of money. The net in your pocket is very different, says Barre. And, he adds, people who have grown used to the zero-tax life "are not used to administrative formalities anymore – tax returns, documents – so it's not easy." More like this: • Dubai's tourism industry reels from 'brutal' impact of war • Why more Americans are now moving to Ireland • Is New York's cannabis business really flying high? "It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE," says Henley & Partners' Peter Ferrigno. "But I think it's far too early for people to wholesale uproot their life when it involves work, family, etc. The vast majority of people in the UAE are still regular people doing regular jobs, even most of the millionaires are millionaires because they are doing well paid jobs rather than being asset owners. If the war is relatively short, they will remain. If it drags on, then people will inevitably look elsewhere, or relocate the family and work remotely until it's safer. If you're in the UAE for work, there aren't likely to be that many equivalent roles in Italy," he says. However, it is likely that the war in the Middle East will dissuade many rich Europeans who would have otherwise moved there from re-locating to the UAE. Last year, Dubai was the number one destination by far for migrating millionaires, according to Henley & Partners. That number is bound to tumble in 2026, and with its attractive offer for the very wealthy, as well as its reputation for  la dolce vita  of course, it may well be Italy that benefits. -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights.  For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . 罗伯特自称只是“中等富裕”，在计算机行业打拼并以出售公司告终后，八年前移居意大利。罗伯特（非真名）或许不在为逃避法国税务而逃往意大利的法国亿万富翁之列，但对他来说，好处显而易见。如果他在法国买房，就必须支付法国人所谓的公证费，其中大部分上缴政府（类似英国的印花税或美国的房产转让税）。而在意大利，首套住房可享豁免。

在法国，马克龙总统将财富税转变为房地产财富税，因此股票市场投资等不再受影响，但“如果你拥有价值一千万美元的房产，这项税确实非常痛苦，”罗伯特说。而意大利没有类似税种。在法国，你还必须缴纳房产税或土地税。“我们这里对首套住房没有这种税，”罗伯特说，不过他指出“垃圾收集费很高”。在他看来，最大的好处是，在意大利拥有的房产，价值高达100万欧元（约110万美元）的部分免征遗产税，超出部分仅征收4%。而在法国，免税限额要低得多——10万欧元（约11万美元）——超出部分按累进税率最高达45%。

"When you are in a country where you do not pay any tax, it's very difficult to come back to a country where you have to pay a lot. Especially for those used to spending a lot of money. readings.title: A sad country song about Texas could become the biggest hit ever
body: Podcasts A sad country song about Texas could become the biggest hit ever ﻿Is “Choosin’ Texas” the song of the summer? by Ariana Aspuru and Noel King Aug 29, 2026, 11:00 AM UTC Gift Ella Langley performs at a country music festival in Nashville, Tennessee, on June 4, 2026. Jason Kempin/Getty Images If you haven’t yet heard about how a certain fella is choosin’ a woman from Texas over Ella Langley, it’s only a matter of time. Langley’s massive hit, “ Choosin’ Texas ,” began dominating the Billboard Hot 100 charts a few months ago — and never looked back. It’s still sitting at No. 1 after 19 weeks, tied for the longest time spent atop the charts among non-holiday songs. In a few more weeks, Langley could shatter the all-time record and dethrone Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You.” It’s a runaway success for Langley, who is relatively new to country music but has quickly vaulted to a new tier of stardom. To break down how it happened, Today, Explained turned to Marissa Moss , a senior writer at Rolling Stone and the author of Her Country: How the Women of Country Music Became the Success They Were Never Supposed to Be . Moss talked with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about where Langley’s success came from, what it means for women in country music, and why many fans don’t know what to make of Langley, who has maintained a low profile for a star artist. Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .

Tell me about “Choosin’ Texas.” “Choosin’ Texas” is a song about a woman who is essentially losing her man in real time. She goes to a bar or a honky-tonk in Texas. She’s from Tennessee. She suddenly realizes that he sees his ex who’s from Texas and drifts away from her to this woman. It’s that feeling of knowing when you see it in someone’s face that they’re going to be leaving you and figuring out whether it’s worth it to hold on or to let go. How big is this song, exactly? It is huge. It is up there right now in competition with Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” which owns the record for the most weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 with 22 weeks. Her only [other] competition is from Shaboozey and Lil Nas X, which are country-adjacent songs. She really could blow by Mariah Carey. Of course you get a boost every time Christmas comes around, but we’re a little ways off from Mariah Carey declaring once and for all that it’s Christmas season. So I think Ella has plenty of time to catch up. And it could be the biggest song of all time, which is crazy. You’re a music writer and you’re based in Nashville. How big a deal is Ella Langley in a place like Nashville and in the country industry? She’s a big deal. And it’s exciting because she’s a relatively newish artist in terms of how long she’s been putting out music. She only released her debut album in 2024, called Hungover . It’s really exciting because as a lot of people know, it can be really hard for a woman to make it in Nashville. Usually under 10 percent of songs on country radio are by women, so having someone like her out there and having so much country radio airplay and presence on the Hot 100 and breaking all these records, you really hope that it’s going to help influence people in Nashville to sign more women, platform more women, do all of those things to try to sort of flip this longstanding sexism that has existed in Nashville. Not to put all of our hopes and dreams on one woman, because it’s not up to her to do this. It’s up to the industry to respond. But you sure have to hope so. Was it a surprise that “Choosin’ Texas” became such a big hit? I would’ve never predicted this. I loved the song when I heard it, but I don’t think I ever thought that something this country could be this popular. “Despite the lyrical content, which may be a little bit of a bummer, the song does just feel so good. And it’s like a little bit of a brain weed gummy.” And yes, country music is becoming so much more popular nationwide, worldwide. But it is also country music in a lot of ways that is a little bit more pop-leaning. Morgan Wallen is extremely popular, but he’s not putting out super-twangy tears-in-your-beer kind of country music songs. “Choosin’ Texas” is kind of sad, but more than sad, I think it’s relatable. It taps into this feeling that a lot of people have, especially in the summer. If you’re thinking about a summer romance, of losing something that you once had, of letting go, of nostalgia, I think that’s something that we really want to feel right now. And despite the lyrical content, which may be a little bit of a bummer, the song does just feel so good. And it’s like a little bit of a brain weed gummy. The second it comes on and you hear that little guitar lick it relaxes you. It gives you that summer feel of airy and fresh and a lot of people want to feel that way right now. You’ve said she’s not a person who shares a ton about herself. Probably smart in this day and age. But country music often does get politicized. And I’ve seen that happening a bit around her and around this song. Tell me about the way she is being slotted into certain perspectives in the US, whether she wants to be or not. One thing I’ve seen is a lot of people from the far right wanting to use her as an example of a return to sort of this anti-girlboss era. They like to take the fact that she speaks about her faith on stage and warp that into that being sort of her overriding agenda and that she wants this return to traditional values. And then on the left, I’ve seen some people sort of play with the same. I personally think you could just as easily make a case that she’s a feminist who had Miranda Lambert produce her album and writes with women and takes all these women on tour. So many people want this moment to serve their own narrative and want Ella Langley to stand for something on every side. And if you don’t give people a little, they’re going to go wild. But maybe that’s better than putting your personal views out there and having them ripped apart. I can’t say I really blame her, to be honest. ##段落
播客：一首关于德克萨斯的悲伤乡村歌曲可能成为史上最热门歌曲。“Choosin’ Texas”会是今夏之歌吗？作者：Ariana Aspuru 和 Noel King，2026年8月29日，上午11:00 UTC。赠品：Ella Langley于2026年6月4日在田纳西州纳什维尔的一个乡村音乐节上演出。图片来源：Jason Kempin/Getty Images。如果你还没听说过某个家伙如何选择一位来自德克萨斯的女人而非Ella Langley，那只是时间问题。Langley的热门单曲“Choosin’ Texas”几个月前开始霸占Billboard Hot 100榜单——并且一路势不可挡。它连续19周稳居榜首，与非节日歌曲的最长登顶时间持平。再过几周，Langley可能打破历史纪录，取代Mariah Carey的“All I Want for Christmas Is You”。这对Langley来说是巨大的成功，她在乡村音乐界相对新人，但迅速跃升至新的明星层级。为了剖析这一切是如何发生的，《今日解释》采访了《滚石》杂志资深撰稿人兼《她的乡村：乡村音乐女性如何成为她们本不该成为的成功》一书的作者Marissa Moss。Moss与《今日解释》联合主持人Noel King讨论了Langley成功的来源、这对乡村音乐女性意味着什么，以及为什么许多粉丝对这位保持低调的明星艺人感到困惑。以下是对话节选，经过编辑以确保长度和清晰度。完整播客内容更多，请在任何获取播客的平台收听《今日解释》，包括Apple Podcasts、Pandora和Spotify。

##段落
给我讲讲“Choosin’ Texas”这首歌。“Choosin’ Texas”是一首关于一个女人在实时失去她的男人的歌曲。她来自田纳西州，去德克萨斯州的一个酒吧或乡村音乐酒吧。她突然意识到他看到了来自德克萨斯的前女友，并逐渐从她身边漂向那个女人。那种感觉就是，当你从某人的脸上看到他们将要离开你时，你会知道，并要判断是值得坚持还是放手。

##段落
这首歌到底有多火？它非常火。目前它正与Mariah Carey的“All I Want for Christmas Is You”竞争，后者以22周位居Billboard Hot 100榜首而保持纪录。她唯一的其他竞争来自Shaboozey和Lil Nas X，这些都是乡村风格的歌曲。她真的可能超越Mariah Carey。当然，每到圣诞节你都会得到提振，但我们离Mariah Carey最终宣布圣诞季到来还有一段时间。所以我认为Ella有足够的时间赶上。它可能成为有史以来最热门的歌曲，这太疯狂了。

##段落
你是一位音乐作家，常驻纳什维尔。在像纳什维尔这样的地方，Ella Langley有多大影响？

她在乡村音乐界是个大人物吗？她可是相当厉害。而且令人兴奋的是，就她发布音乐的时间长度而言，她算是个相对较新的艺人。她直到2024年才发行了她的首张专辑，名叫《宿醉》。这真的很令人兴奋，因为众所周知，女性在纳什维尔取得成功非常困难。通常，乡村电台播放的歌曲中，女性演唱的不到10%，所以能有她这样的人出现，在乡村电台获得如此多的播放量，进入热门100榜，打破所有这些纪录，你真的希望这能影响纳什维尔的人们去签约更多女性，为更多女性提供平台，做所有这些事情，试图扭转纳什维尔长期存在的性别歧视。不是说要把我们所有的希望和梦想都寄托在一个女人身上，因为这不是她一个人的责任，而是行业需要做出回应。但你当然希望如此。《选择德克萨斯》成为如此大热单曲，这让你意外吗？我从未预料到这一点。我听到这首歌时就喜欢它，但我从没想过这么乡村风格的东西能这么流行。“尽管歌词内容可能有点让人沮丧，但这首歌听起来就是感觉很好。它就像一点大脑软糖。”是的，乡村音乐在全国乃至全球正变得越来越流行。但在很多方面，乡村音乐也开始偏向流行风格。摩根·沃伦非常火，但他并不是在发布那种超级乡村、悲情入骨的“泪洒啤酒”式歌曲。《选择德克萨斯》有点悲伤，但与其说是悲伤，不如说我觉得它很能引起共鸣。它触及了很多人，尤其是夏天时，常有的那种感觉。如果你在想着夏日恋情，想着失去曾经拥有的东西，想着放手，想着怀旧，我觉得这正是我们现在真正想感受的。尽管歌词内容可能有点让人沮丧，但这首歌听起来就是感觉很好。它就像一点大脑软糖。一响起来，你听到那小小的吉他拨弦声，就会放松下来。它给你那种轻盈、清新的夏日感觉，而很多人现在就想这样。“你曾说她不是一个会分享太多关于自己的事的人。在这个时代，这可能是明智的。但乡村音乐常常被政治化。我注意到围绕她和这首歌，这种情况开始出现。告诉我她如何被定位在美国的某些视角中，不管她是否愿意。我看到的一件事是，很多极右翼人士想把她当作回归反女强人时代的例子。他们喜欢利用她在舞台上谈论信仰这一点，把它扭曲成某种……她的标志性特征。

压倒性的议程是她希望回归传统价值观。而在左翼方面，我看到一些人也在玩同样的把戏。我个人认为，你同样可以轻易地论证她是一位女权主义者——她让米兰达·兰伯特制作专辑，与女性合作写歌，并带着这些女性一起巡演。太多人希望这一刻服务于自己的叙事，希望艾拉·兰利在每一方都能代表某种立场。如果你不给他们一点甜头，他们就会发狂。但也许这比把自己的个人观点抛出去然后被撕碎要好。说实话，我不能说我真的责怪她。

readings.title: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
body: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
We persist in hiring and training as if we’re running a bowling squad, as if easily measured skills are all that matter.

What causes successful organizations to fail ? What makes stocks fade, innovations slow, customers jump ship? We can agree that certain skills are essential. That hiring coders who can’t code, salespeople who can’t sell, or architects who can’t design is a waste. But these skills — let’s call them vocational skills — have become the backbone of the recruitment process.

But how do you explain that similar organizations, with similarly vocationally skilled people, find themselves with very different outcomes? Most of the textbooks that students experience and the tests they take are about vocational skills, the checkboxes that have to be checked to get a job. By misdefining “vocational” and focusing on these allegedly essential skills, we’ve diminished the value of the other skills that matter.

We give too little respect to the other skills when we call them “soft” and imply that they’re optional. What actually separates thriving organizations from struggling ones are the difficult-to-measure attitudes, processes and perceptions of the people who do the work.

Vocational skills can be taught: You’re not born knowing engineering or copywriting or even graphic design, therefore they must be something we can teach. But we let ourselves off the hook when it comes to decision-making, eager participation, dancing with fear, speaking with authority, working in teams , seeing the truth, speaking the truth, inspiring others, doing more than we’re asked, caring and being willing to change things. We underinvest in this training, fearful that these things are innate and can’t be taught. Perhaps they’re talents. And so we downplay them, calling them soft skills, making it easy for us to move on to something seemingly more urgent.

At scale, organizations pay less attention to soft skills when hiring because we’ve persuaded ourselves that vocational skills are impersonal and easier to measure. If it’s easier to test for, it seems more important when selecting our team.
And we fire slowly (and retrain rarely) when these skills are missing, because we’re worried about stepping on toes, being called out for getting personal or possibly wasting time on a lost cause.

But these skills can all be learned, as obvious skills like chess or typing can be learned. We learn them accidentally, by osmosis, by the collisions we have with teachers, parents, bosses and the world. Even though they’re more difficult to measure, that doesn’t mean we can’t improve them, can’t practice them or can’t change the way we do our work.

Let’s stop calling them soft. They’re interpersonal skills. Leadership skills. The skills of charisma and diligence and contribution. But these modifiers, while accurate, somehow edge them away from the vocational skills, the skills that we actually hire for, the skills we measure a graduate degree on.
So let’s uncomfortably call them real skills instead.
Real because they work, because they’re at the heart of what we need today.
Real because even if you’ve got the vocational skills, you’re no help to us without these human skills, the things that we can’t write down or program a computer to do.
Real skills can’t replace vocational skills, of course. What they can do is amplify the things you’ve already been measuring.
Imagine a team member with all the traditional vocational skills: productive, skilled, experienced. A resume that can prove it. That’s a fine baseline.

Now add to it. Perceptive, charismatic, driven, focused, goal-setting, inspiring and motivated. Generous, empathic and consistent. A deep listener , with patience. What happens to your organization when someone like that joins your team?
Writing in the Harvard Business Review , Lou Solomon reports that 69 percent of managers are uncomfortable communicating with their employees. I’d guess that many of the other 31 percent are lying.

Communicating with employees is uncomfortable because we’ve built systems of compliance and dominance that make it difficult. We ask people to leave their humanity at the door, then use authority to change behavior. We overlay corporate greed and short-term thinking with a human desire to create work that matters.

How do we build people-centric organizations while also accepting the fact that two thirds of our managers (presumably well paid, well trained and integral to our success) are so uncomfortable doing an essential part of their job that they admitted it to a stranger?

In a recent survey, the Graduate Management Admission Council reported that although MBAs were strong in analytical aptitude, quantitative expertise and information-gathering ability, they were sorely lacking in other critical areas that employers find equally attractive: strategic thinking, written and oral communication, leadership and adaptability . Are these mutually exclusive? Must we trade one for the other?

The foundation of all real skills is this one: the confidence and permission to talk to one another. Not to manage, belittle, intimidate or control. Simply to seek to be understood and to do the work to understand.

##段落
让我们停止称它们为“软技能”——改称“真实技能”吧  
2023年6月9日  
/  
赛斯·戈丁  
/  
Facebook  
X  
LinkedIn  
Reddit  
WhatsApp  
黛博拉·斯皮尔曼  
我们依然像经营保龄球队一样进行招聘和培训，仿佛只有易于衡量的技能才重要。

##段落
是什么导致成功组织走向失败？是什么让股价黯淡、创新放缓、客户流失？我们可以达成共识：某些技能至关重要。雇佣不会编程的程序员、不会销售的销售员、或不会设计的建筑师，纯属浪费。但这些技能——不妨称之为职业技能——已成为招聘流程的支柱。

##段落
但如何解释那些拥有相似职业技能人才、结构相似的组织，最终却走向截然不同的结局？学生所经历的多数教科书和考试，都围绕职业技能，即求职时必须勾选的条条框框。通过错误定义“职业性”并聚焦于这些所谓关键技能，我们贬低了其他真正重要的技能的价值。

##段落
当我们称其他技能为“软”技能，暗示它们是可选项时，就给予了它们太少的尊重。真正将蓬勃发展组织与挣扎求生组织区分开来的，是那些难以衡量的态度、流程和从业者的认知。

##段落
职业技能是可以传授的：你并非天生就懂工程、文案或平面设计，因此它们必是可教之物。但在决策、积极投入、与恐惧共舞、有权威地表达、团队协作、看清真相、说出真相、激励他人、超出要求地付出、关怀他人以及愿意推动变革这些方面，我们却让自己轻易脱身。我们在这方面投资不足，担心这些特质是天生的、无法教导。也许它们是天赋。于是我们淡化它们，称之为软技能，好让自己轻松转向看似更紧迫的事务。

##段落
在规模化运作中，组织在招聘时较少关注软技能，因为我们说服自己：职业技能是非人格化的、更容易衡量。如果更容易测试，在选拔团队时它就显得更重要。

##段落
而当这些技能缺失时，我们又迟迟不辞退（也极少再培训），因为担心踩到别人的脚、被指摘过于针对个人，或是在无望的事情上浪费时间。

##段落
但这些技能全都可以习得，就像下棋或打字这类显而易见的技能一样可以学会。我们通过偶然机会、潜移默化、以及与老师、父母、老板和世界的碰撞而学到它们。尽管它们更难衡量，但这并不意味着我们无法改进、无法练习——

我们不能改变我们的工作方式吗？  
当然可以。  
让我们别再称它们为“软技能”了。它们是人际交往技能。领导力技能。是魅力、勤奋和贡献的技能。但这些修饰词，虽然准确，却不知怎地把它们推离了职业技能，那些我们真正招聘时看重、用研究生学位衡量的技能。  
所以，让我们不舒服地称它们为“真实技能”吧。  
说它们真实，是因为它们有效，因为它们是我们今天所需的核心。  
说它们真实，是因为即使你拥有职业技能，没有这些人类技能——那些我们无法写下来或编程让计算机去做的事——你对我们毫无帮助。  
真实技能当然不能取代职业技能。它们能做的是放大你已经在衡量的那些东西。  
想象一个拥有所有传统职业技能的团队成员：高效、熟练、经验丰富。一份能证明这一点的简历。那是一个不错的基线。  
现在加上这些：洞察力强、有魅力、有驱动力、专注、目标明确、能激励他人、自我激励。慷慨、富有同理心、始终如一。深度倾听，且有耐心。当这样的人加入你的团队时，你的组织会发生什么？  
在《哈佛商业评论》上，卢·所罗门报道称，69%的管理者不善于与员工沟通。我猜另外31%中的许多人都在撒谎。  
与员工沟通之所以令人不适，是因为我们建立了顺从和支配的系统，使沟通变得困难。我们要求人们把人性留在门外，然后用权威来改变行为。我们将企业贪婪和短期思维与创造有意义工作的人类愿望叠加在一起。  
我们如何建立以人为本的组织，同时接受这样一个事实：我们三分之二的管理者（想必薪酬优厚、训练有素、对我们的成功至关重要）对执行其工作的基本部分如此不适，以至于他们向陌生人承认了这一点？  
在最近的一项调查中，研究生入学管理委员会报告称，尽管MBA在分析能力、定量专业知识和信息收集能力方面很强，但他们在雇主同样重视的其他关键领域严重欠缺：战略思维、书面和口头沟通、领导力和适应性。这些是相互排斥的吗？我们必须用一项换取另一项吗？  
所有真实技能的基础是这一项：彼此交谈的自信和许可。不是为了管理、贬低、恐吓或控制。仅仅是为了寻求被理解，并努力去理解。  
摘自塞斯·高汀的《意义之歌：团队新宣言》，经企鹅兰登书屋旗下Portfolio出版社同意。

readings.title: How social media ceased to be social
body: 22 May 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Social media platforms used to be about communication between friends – now many are increasingly short video entertainment hubs. The business model is to increase the time people spend on their apps and increase ad revenue. But is there already a consumer backlash? Aurélia fixes herself a coffee, sits down in her beautiful garden not far from Paris and goes on Instagram "to relax." First up: "a guy I like a lot who does interior design. He's in Venice at the moment." She's into interior design, and has even just had two bird drawings by the 19th Century English designer William Morris tattooed on her arms. She scrolls down. Two kittens having a fight. "I love animals so I get a lot of animals. That's how it works, social media. You click on bananas and they give you bananas." There are ads too – although they look just like the other posts – for a robot-vacuum cleaner, a diet and bed linen (with Morris-inspired designs). But no friends. She has 198 on Instagram but she says "it's completely changed. I practically don’t see any friends' posts anymore." She’s pretty much given up posting herself. "I don't think anyone sees them anymore anyway."  While there remain committed social, amateur posters on Instagram and especially Facebook, the switch from communicating with people you know to scrolling through professionally made content from people you don't, is even more pronounced among young users. Kylian, 16, is in vocational training to become a chef. He's on TikTok and Youtube a lot, he says. "I like looking at videos more than photos or messages. I watch videos made by people I don't know. I don’t post at all. I'm a rather shy person. I stay in my bubble. I watch and that’s all. I keep my reactions to myself." "I spend a lot of time scrolling through videos made by content-creators," says Lucie, also 16. "They're more interesting than the posts of people I know." She doesn't post except sometimes "stories" which disappear after 24 hours.  Whether it's TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and Instagram, we are a long way from the "digital town square" of personal interaction that social media was even just a few years ago. In France, annual official Barometre du numerique 2026  shows 49% of social media users are "active only occasionally". In the UK, an Ofcom report   published in April showed a year-on-year drop of users who actively post from 61% to 49%. In the US, a Morning Consult survey of June last year found 28% reported posting less often than the previous year. Just 33% now post daily compared to 57% who use it for entertainment daily. The gap is a lot wider still for Gen Z – 18% active for 74% passive. Vanessa Lalo, a Paris-based clinical psychologist specialising in on-line behaviour, says "users have become more conscious that the traces you leave (on social media) stay there forever and some no longer want to maintain social media relations that can be superficial. Some don’t want the exposure to criticism that might be a risk when you post or the feeling that their post will seem poor alongside all the professional content". However, Lalo adds, people haven’t stopped posting, rather they are posting different things and in different places. "On TikTok, for example, young people publish a lot of content but it's more funny parodies and remixes of existing material. The goal is to make people laugh, not to tell people about their lives." That still happens, she says, but it’s moved from social media platforms like Instagram and Facebook to messaging sites like WhatsApp. There's also been a move towards private groups on Instagram and Snapchat. "These are much more intimate places where you're not bombarded with ads and content made by influencers," she says. "What we're seeing is social media splitting in two," says social media consultant Matt Navarra, author of the Geekout Newsletter. "Big platforms like Instagram and TikTok are becoming more about entertainment and discovery. WhatsApp is becoming the place people go to actually be social. The catch is, those kinds of spaces are harder for companies to make money from." Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business – Matt Navarra It was TikTok that helped to pioneer an algorithm that figures out from the moment you start scrolling what you like, and then fills your feed with material calculated to keep you on the app for the longest possible time. Now, says Matt Navarra, "Meta has built what it calls an AI system for unconnected content recommendations on Facebook and Instagram, which basically means, they're increasingly showing you stuff from people you don't follow because the machine thinks you're going to like it. It's not biased towards, is it a professional creator? Is it a brand? Is it a friend? If they can see that you've engaged with a friend a lot, you might see a lot more of their content. It's just that who you are friends with, who you follow, has become irrelevant in a way." This all means that small businesses, that have long used social media for free promotion have to up their game.   "There's a real opportunity for some small businesses," says Matt Navarra. "A bakery, florist, salon or local café can still break through if they have a good story, strong visuals or behind-the-scenes content people want to watch. But it also means the job has changed. Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business." The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow – Matt Navarra Social media is evolving into something passive like television, albeit television that adapts as you zap. Or rather which knows you so well that it doesn't seem to matter that much that it's taken the remote control. You give the platform information about yourself that it uses for commercial gain and, in return, it gives you content tailored to please you for free. The transition from truly social media to entertainment platform does seem to be paying off. "The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow," says Matt Navarra. Global social media ad revenue is expected to reach $317 billion (£236bn) in 2026, up from $277 billion (£206bn) last year. Meta is the biggest winner. Its ad sales already increased 22% year-on-year in 2025.  Ad sales are expected to hit $243 billion (£181bn) this year , enough to overtake Google for the first time. AI powered digital ad targeting is becoming ever more effective and precise. "The social platforms allow companies to put ads amongst the content that you're scrolling through. Every third or fourth scroll is an ad. And they are the world's best ad targeting engines. They know so much about your interests because of what you've looked at, liked, engaged with, what you've chosen to follow, the time you've spent in certain areas of the app, things like that," Navarra says.  "So advertisers will go in and say: 'I want to place an ad next to people in the UK who are between thirty and sixty years old and who are interested in DIY' and the social platforms will have that information and will place the ads accordingly." The price will depend on the number of impressions (clicks) the advertiser wants and how tight the criteria are. It costs more to place ads in the social media feeds of people who buy horses than people who buy ice-cream. More like this: •  TikTok is tracking you, even if you don't use the app. Here's how to stop it •  How to stop AI from turning your brain to mush •  This monkey selfie will protect you from AI slop Might there be a backlash coming? Don't many people go on to social media to see how friends are reacting to their posts or comments before settling down to scroll through professionally made content? Whether it's the shrinking social motivation to get on these apps or something else, the amount of time people spend on social media plateaued at an average of 141 minutes in 2025, down slightly from 143 minutes in 2024 . However, this is only part of the story, as the number of people using social media and the total time humanity spends on these apps continues to rise. For Gen Z it’s higher still. Around five hours a day in the United States where, for this demographic, social media has also become the primary search engine and shopping tool. Meanwhile, for those who miss what are fast becoming the old days when social media enabled you to share a bit of your life, a joke or a point of view with people you more-or-less knew, there are tools within platforms, says Matt Navarra, that allow you to choose to see mainly friends and family content. "People can flick to a feed that gives them that," he says. "But most people don't." -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.   For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . 社交媒体平台曾经是关于朋友之间交流的——如今许多平台日益成为短视频娱乐中心。其商业模式是增加人们在应用上花费的时间，并增加广告收入。但消费者是否已经开始产生抵制情绪？

奥蕾莉亚给自己泡了一杯咖啡，坐在巴黎附近美丽的花园里，上Instagram“放松一下”。首先映入眼帘的是：“我非常喜欢的一个做室内设计的家伙。他现在在威尼斯。”她热衷于室内设计，甚至刚刚把19世纪英国设计师威廉·莫里斯的两幅鸟类画作纹在手臂上。她向下滑动屏幕。两只小猫在打架。“我喜欢动物，所以看到很多动物内容。社交媒体就是这样运作的。你点击香蕉，他们就给你看香蕉。”也有广告——尽管它们看起来和其他帖子一模一样——比如扫地机器人、减肥餐和床单（带有莫里斯风格的设计）。但没有朋友。她在Instagram上有198个粉丝，但她说“情况完全变了。我几乎再也看不到任何朋友的帖子了。”她自己也基本不再发帖了。“我觉得反正也没人看了。”

虽然在Instagram尤其是Facebook上，仍然有热衷于社交的业余发帖者，但从与认识的人交流转向浏览陌生人的专业制作内容，这一转变在年轻用户中尤为明显。16岁的基利安正在接受厨师职业培训。他说自己经常刷TikTok和YouTube。“我喜欢看视频胜过看照片或消息。我看不认识的人制作的视频。我完全不发帖。我是个比较害羞的人。我待在自己的小圈子里。我只是看，仅此而已。我把自己的反应藏在心里。”

“我花很多时间刷内容创作者制作的视频，”同为16岁的露西说。“它们比我认识的人发的帖子更有趣。”她不发帖，只是偶尔发一些24小时后消失的“快拍”。

无论是TikTok、Snapchat、Facebook还是Instagram，我们早已远离了社交媒体几年前还是个人互动的“数字城市广场”的状态。在法国，2026年官方年度《数字晴雨表》显示，49%的社交媒体用户“仅偶尔活跃”。在英国，4月发布的Ofcom报告显示，积极发帖的用户同比下降了12个百分点，从61%降至49%。在美国，去年6月Morning Consult的一项调查发现，28%的受访者表示发帖频率比前一年减少了。目前只有33%的人每天发帖，而57%的人每天使用社交媒体进行娱乐。Z世代的差距更大——18%的人积极发帖，而74%的人被动浏览。瓦内萨·拉洛，一位驻巴黎的临床心理学家，专攻在线行为领域

她说：“用户已经意识到，你在社交媒体上留下的痕迹会永远存在，有些人不再想维持可能肤浅的社交媒体关系。有些人不想暴露在发帖时可能面临的批评风险，也不想感觉自己的帖子在专业内容面前显得逊色。”然而，拉洛补充说，人们并没有停止发帖，而是发布不同的内容，在不同的地方发布。“例如，在TikTok上，年轻人发布大量内容，但更多是滑稽的模仿和对现有素材的混搭。目标是让人们发笑，而不是讲述自己的生活。”她说，分享生活仍然存在，但已从Instagram和Facebook等社交媒体平台转移到WhatsApp等即时通讯网站。同时，人们也转向Instagram和Snapchat上的私密群组。“这些是更私密的空间，你不会被广告和网红内容轰炸，”她说。

##段落

“我们看到的是社交媒体正在一分为二，”社交媒体顾问、Geekout Newsletter作者马特·纳瓦拉说。“像Instagram和TikTok这样的大平台正变得更侧重于娱乐和发现。WhatsApp正在成为人们真正进行社交的地方。问题在于，这类空间对公司来说更难盈利。”——正是TikTok率先开创了一种算法，从你开始浏览的那一刻起就能判断你的喜好，然后填充你的信息流，以计算好的内容让你尽可能长时间留在应用上。马特·纳瓦拉说，现在，“Meta已经在其Facebook和Instagram上构建了所谓的AI系统，用于不相关内容的推荐，这基本上意味着，它们越来越多地向你展示你未关注的人的内容，因为机器认为你会喜欢。它不会偏向于这是专业创作者、品牌还是朋友。如果机器发现你与某位朋友互动频繁，你可能会看到更多他们的内容。只是，你的朋友是谁、你关注谁，在某种程度上已变得无关紧要。”这一切意味着，长期利用社交媒体免费推广的小企业必须提升自己的水平。

##段落

“一些小企业确实有机会，”马特·纳瓦拉说。“面包店、花店、沙龙或本地咖啡馆，如果有好故事、强烈的视觉或人们想看的幕后内容，仍然可以脱颖而出。但这同时也意味着工作方式已改变。小企业主正被迫成为主持人、编辑、潮流发现者和内容创作者，同时还要管理实际业务。”——马特·纳瓦拉

##段落
实际上经营业务的核心。"社交平台仍然主要通过广告收入实现商业化，这依然是核心商业模式，而广告收入持续增长——马特·纳瓦拉
##段落
社交媒体正在演变成像电视一样被动的东西，尽管是那种在你换台时会自我适应的电视。或者更准确地说，它如此了解你，以至于它拿走了遥控器这件事似乎也没那么重要了。你向平台提供关于自己的信息，平台用这些信息谋取商业利益，作为回报，它免费为你提供量身定制的、让你愉悦的内容。从真正的社交媒体向娱乐平台的转变似乎确实在奏效。"社交平台仍然主要通过广告收入实现商业化，这依然是核心商业模式，而广告收入持续增长，"马特·纳瓦拉表示。全球社交媒体广告收入预计将从去年的2770亿美元（2060亿英镑）增长至2026年的3170亿美元（2360亿英镑）。Meta是最大的赢家，其广告销售额在2025年已经同比增长22%，预计今年将达到2430亿美元（1810亿英镑），足以首次超越谷歌。
##段落
AI驱动的数字广告定向投放正变得前所未有的高效和精准。"社交平台允许企业在你浏览的内容中插入广告，每滚动三四次就会看到一条广告。它们是全球最好的广告定向引擎，因为它们通过你查看过、点赞过、互动过的内容，你选择关注的对象，你在应用特定区域停留的时间等等，对你的兴趣了如指掌，"纳瓦拉说。"所以广告主会过来说：'我想把广告投放在英国30到60岁、对DIY感兴趣的用户旁边'，社交平台掌握这些信息，就会相应地投放广告。"价格取决于广告主想要的展示次数（点击量）以及筛选条件的精准程度。在购买马匹的人群的社交媒体信息流中投放广告，比在购买冰淇淋的人群中投放要贵得多。
##段落
更多类似内容：• TikTok在追踪你，即使你不用这款应用，以下是阻止方法 • 如何防止AI把你的大脑变成一团浆糊 • 这张猴子自拍照将保护你免受AI垃圾内容侵害
##段落
是否会有反弹来临？难道不是很多人先上社交媒体看看朋友对自己的帖子或评论有何反应，然后才安下心来浏览专业制作的内容吗？无论是上这些应用的社交动机在减弱，还是其他原因，人们在社交媒体上花费的时间在2025年趋于平稳，平均为141分钟，比2024年的143分钟略有下降。然而，这只是故事的一部分，因为使用社交媒体的人数仍在增长——

全球范围内，人们在社交媒体上花费的总时间持续攀升。对于Z世代而言，这一数字更高，在美国每天约达五小时，社交媒体已成为这一群体的主要搜索引擎和购物工具。与此同时，对于那些怀念社交媒体最初功能——与熟人分享生活片段、笑话或观点——的人来说，平台内已有工具可选择主要查看朋友和家人的内容，马特·纳瓦拉指出。“人们可以切换到这样的信息流，”他说，“但大多数人并不这么做。”——若您喜欢此故事，请订阅《必读清单》通讯，每周两次精选特稿、视频和不容错过的新闻，直接发送至您的邮箱。如需更多商业及更多领域资讯，请在领英上关注我们。商业科技特稿社交媒体商业世界

readings.title: The bears cooling off in a California pool
body: 16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Isabelle Gerretsen Black bears love lounging in Brian Gordon and Ricardo Martinez's pool in Los Angeles. As bear encounters increase across Southern California, the couple share videos of their furry visitors and reveal how they are co-existing with these wild animals. When Brian Gordon first learned that black bears were swimming in the pool of the house he was buying in Los Angeles, he was very afraid. "I'd never seen a bear in real life. I said, 'We'll just build a big wall with barbed wire,'" he recalls. Four years later, Gordon loves nothing more than seeing a family of bears playing in his pool and running around his garden. The furry visitors stop by several times a week. (Scroll down to watch a video of the bears at play.) "They are fine to come here and scratch on the trees, take a nap, and jump in the pool if it's hot, as long as we're not creating harm for them, or for ourselves," Gordon says. Gordon and his partner Ricardo Martinez have made it their mission to peacefully share their pool and garden with the bears. But behind these charming videos of bears relaxing in their pool, there's a deeper story of vigilance and safety precautions that make this co-existence possible. The couple live in Monrovia, Los Angeles County, in Southern California, home to around 1,600 bears . Their house is in the foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains and borders the Angeles National Forest, which spans 700,000 acres (2,830sq km). When the couple moved in, they started spotting bears almost immediately. They initially tried to chase the bears away by yelling, using air horns and occasionally a paintball gun with soft rubber pellets. "But it felt horrible," says Martinez. "It did not sit right with us. We said that as long as they're not breaking into the home and getting into the trash, then they're ok to come by." They sought an approach that would keep both themselves and the bears safe, despite close proximity. "We've since settled on less aggressive means, and honestly, they work better for us," says Gordon. We have had bears crashing barbecues – Brian Gordon Martinez says that black bears are "misunderstood". "They are not going to eat you," says Martinez. Black bear attacks are incredibly rare, with just one fatal attack recorded in California's history .  The couple say they always keep a "healthy distance" from the bears and stay inside when the animals are around. There are sometimes unplanned encounters though.  "We have had bears crashing barbecues," says Gordon. "But if they see you, they usually just walk away." Gordon and Martinez say their favourite bear visitor is Maddie, who they first got to know as an incredibly inquisitive youngster in 2023. She loved playing in the pool and hanging around the garden. "She is our golden child," says Martinez. A year later, Maddie returned with her cubs in tow. "Unfortunately she lost those cubs, so we went through an emotional rollercoaster with her," says Martinez. This year she has brought her new cubs to the house. "They're the most adorable [creatures] you've ever seen. They're so cuddly but also intimidating, with their long claws." We live here and the bears live here. We don't want them to go anywhere – Ricardo Martinez Punky is another "rambunctious yearling" who first came to the house as a cub with her mother, says Gordon. "She would pop all the pool floaties." She once climbed onto an inflatable cupcake and drifted into the middle of the pool. "She really stole our hearts that summer with her pool fun," says Gordon. They nicknamed another regular visitor "Nappy", as the female bear likes to take long siestas while floating in the pool. "She'll literally go to the steps of the pool, get in and put her head down. She's the only bear I've seen take hour-long naps in the pool," says Gordon. If she sees the couple, Nappy will huff at them. "She's a big mama bear and she's just a little grumpy about everything in life," Gordon jokes. These characters are among a growing number of black bears trying to make a home alongside Californians , and often posing challenges for local communities.  There are more than 60,000 black bears living in California , says Wilson Sherman, a research fellow at the University of California, Los Angeles. Black bears are an increasingly common sight in LA suburbs. "They are really intelligent, adaptable omnivores. They eat everything and have learned how to gain calories in places where people live," says Sherman, who studies how communities respond to black bears.  Not all bear encounters are as positive as Gordon and Martinez's experience though. "We do see incidents pretty regularly of bears raiding trash and entering homes," says Sherman. "The really sad thing about this is that when things go awry, it's usually the bears that end up paying the price. Several bears have been put down in the last few years.   A mother black bear called Blondie was euthanised by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife in March 2026 after she swiped at a woman walking her dog in Monrovia.  Blondie had also visited Gordon and Martinez's garden a few times and never caused any problems. Gordon organised a petition to try to prevent the euthanasia, which was signed by almost 6,000 people. "It was pretty devastating. Blondie resembles all mama bears, just trying to find shelter, to raise her kids and live her life," he says. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife says that DNA testing revealed that the captured bear was responsible for the incident, as well as a previous attack on an elderly resident sitting on his porch in Monrovia in June 2025. "Euthanasia is used only as a last resort when an animal poses a risk to public safety and cannot be safely returned to the wild," says a spokesperson. "Relocation may seem like a solution but is not an option when it could put public safety at risk. Bears have strong spatial memory and often return to familiar areas." The bear's cubs are being cared for at a wildlife rehabilitation centre and will be released into a suitable habitat when they are ready, he adds. To minimise conflict with bears, Sherman says it is important that communities restrict access to attractants, such as rubbish bins and leaving food outdoors.  "For a bear, finding a box that's full of pizza when you've been spending your time digging for worms and roots is a game changer." Keeping neighbourhoods bear-free is a "collective training effort", Sherman adds. "You all have to be on the same page, because if one person's leaving a lot of really good stuff in their yard, the bear is very likely going to think, 'I should check out a handful of other yards.'" Gordon says that they are "hypervigilant" when it comes to waste. "We don't even use our trash cans. I haul it to my office, a couple of times a week." They also keep their doors and windows closed and don't ever leave food in their car. They're not teddy bears, they are still wild animals – Wilson Sherman The couple say they have never had a negative encounter with any of the bears visiting their home. Martinez once found Nappy in the garage when he'd accidentally left it open. "We both startled each other," he says. "I slowly walked back, because you don't ever want to corner a bear." She emerged from the garage and went on her way, he says. More like this:
Why grizzly bears need their own hiking trails
The true story of Germany ' s rampant raccoons

Social media accounts, like Martinez and Gordon's, and home surveillance cameras are allowing people "to understand bears as individuals and providing an intimate look into their lives", says Sherman. But he has some reservations. "There's always the risk of Disneyfication, of painting too fuzzy a picture. They're not teddy bears, they are still wild animals." Sherman warns that it is important that bears and humans don't become too comfortable around each other. "Part of loving bears is creating healthy boundaries and setting the bears up for success when they inevitably pass through our neighbourhoods," he says. Through their Instagram account dedicated to the bears, @poolbearlife, Gordon and Martinez hope to raise awareness of how people can behave safely around bears and how to mitigate unwanted encounters. They stress that their relationship with black bears is not something that could necessarily be universal. "This works for us, for where we live," says Gordon.  "It's all about finding that balance with wildlife, how can we co-thrive?" says Martinez. "We live here and the bears live here. We don't want them to go anywhere." -- For essential climate news and hopeful developments to your inbox, sign up to the  Future Earth newsletter, while  The Essential List delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights twice a week.   For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on  Facebook and  Instagram . 16小时前 分享 保存 设为谷歌首选 Isabelle Gerretsen 黑熊喜欢在洛杉矶布莱恩·戈登和里卡多·马丁内斯的泳池里休闲。随着南加州熊出没事件增多，这对夫妇分享了他们毛茸茸访客的视频，并揭示了他们如何与这些野生动物共存。当布莱恩·戈登第一次得知黑熊在他正购买的洛杉矶房子泳池里游泳时，他非常害怕。“我从未在现实中见过熊。我说，‘我们就建一堵带铁丝网的高墙吧，’”他回忆道。四年后，戈登最爱的莫过于看着一家熊在他的泳池里玩耍、在他的花园里跑来跑去。这些毛茸茸的访客每周会来好几次。（向下滚动观看熊玩耍的视频。）“它们来这里抓抓树、打个盹，如果天热就跳进泳池，只要我们不伤害它们，也不伤害自己，就没问题，”戈登说。戈登和他的伴侣里卡多·马丁内斯把与熊和平共享泳池和花园视为己任。但在这些熊在泳池里放松的迷人视频背后，是一个关于警惕和安全预防措施的更深层故事，正是这些让这种共存成为可能。这对夫妇住在南加州洛杉矶县的蒙罗维亚，这里约有1600只熊。他们的房子位于圣加布里埃尔山脉的山麓，毗邻占地70万英亩（2830平方公里）的安吉利斯国家森林。这对夫妇搬进来后，几乎立刻就开始发现熊的踪迹。他们最初尝试通过大喊大叫、使用空气喇叭，偶尔用装有软橡胶弹丸的彩弹枪来驱赶熊。“但感觉糟透了，”马丁内斯说。“我们心里过意不去。我们说，只要它们不闯进家里、不翻垃圾桶，那它们来就没事。”他们寻求一种既能保护自己又能保护熊安全的方法，尽管距离很近。“我们后来采用了不那么激进的手段，老实说，这对我们更有效，”戈登说。我们遇到过熊闯进烧烤聚会的情况——布莱恩·戈登 马丁内斯说，黑熊“被误解了”。“它们不会吃你，”马丁内斯说。黑熊袭击事件极为罕见，加州历史上仅记录过一次致命袭击。这对夫妇说，他们总是与熊保持“安全距离”，当动物在附近时，他们就待在室内。不过，有时也会发生意外的相遇。“我们遇到过熊闯进烧烤聚会的情况，”戈登说。“但如果它们看到你，通常只会走开。”戈登和马丁内斯说，他们最喜欢的熊访客是玛迪，他们在2023年第一次认识她时，她还是个极其好奇的小家伙。她喜欢在泳池里玩耍，也喜欢在周围闲逛。

##段落
绕花园一圈。“她是我们的金童，”马丁内斯说。一年后，麦迪带着她的幼崽回来了。“不幸的是，她失去了那些幼崽，所以我们和她一起经历了情绪上的过山车，”马丁内斯说。今年，她把新生的幼崽带到了房子附近。“它们是你见过的最可爱的[生物]。它们非常惹人喜爱，但也令人心生敬畏，因为它们有长长的爪子。”我们住在这里，熊也住在这里。我们不想让它们去任何地方——里卡多·马丁内斯

##段落
邦基是另一只“精力充沛的一岁熊”，首次作为幼崽随母亲来到房子，戈登说。“她会把所有的泳池浮具都弄破。”她曾经爬上一个充气纸杯蛋糕，漂到泳池中央。“那个夏天，她在泳池里的嬉戏真的俘获了我们的心，”戈登说。他们给另一位常客起了个绰号叫“纳皮”，因为这头母熊喜欢在泳池里漂浮时睡长午觉。“她真的会走到泳池台阶，进去，然后把头低下。她是我见过的唯一一头会在泳池里睡一小时午觉的熊，”戈登说。如果看到这对夫妇，纳皮会朝他们喷气。“她是个大熊妈妈，对生活中的一切都有点脾气暴躁，”戈登开玩笑说。

##段落
这些角色是越来越多的黑熊试图与加州人比邻而居的一部分，这常常给当地社区带来挑战。加州有超过6万只黑熊，加州大学洛杉矶分校研究员威尔逊·谢尔曼说。黑熊在洛杉矶郊区越来越常见。“它们是非常聪明、适应性强的杂食动物。它们什么都吃，并且学会了如何在人类居住的地方获取卡路里，”研究社区如何应对黑熊的谢尔曼说。

##段落
并非所有与熊的相遇都像戈登和马丁内斯的经历那样积极。“我们确实经常看到熊翻垃圾和闯入民宅的事件，”谢尔曼说。“真正令人难过的是，当事情出错时，通常最终付出代价的是熊。过去几年里，有几只熊被处死。”一只名叫布隆迪的母黑熊于2026年3月被加州鱼类和野生动物局实施安乐死，此前她在蒙罗维亚袭击了一名遛狗的女性。布隆迪也曾几次造访戈登和马丁内斯的花园，从未造成任何问题。戈登组织了一份请愿书，试图阻止安乐死，有近6000人签名。“这非常令人心碎。布隆迪和所有熊妈妈一样，只是试图寻找庇护所，抚养她的孩子，过她的生活，”他说。加州鱼类和野生动物局表示，DNA检测显示，被捕获的熊应对该事件负责，以及之前的一起事件。

2025年6月，在蒙罗维亚，一只熊袭击了一位坐在自家门廊上的老年居民。“安乐死仅在动物对公共安全构成威胁且无法安全放归野外时，作为最后手段使用，”一位发言人表示。“重新安置看似是解决方案，但在可能危及公共安全时并非选项。熊具有强烈的空间记忆，往往会返回熟悉的区域。”他补充说，这只熊的幼崽正在一家野生动物康复中心接受照料，待它们准备好后将被释放到合适的栖息地。谢尔曼表示，为尽量减少与熊的冲突，社区限制垃圾箱和户外遗留食物等诱因的接触至关重要。“对于一只熊来说，当你一直挖虫子、啃树根时，发现一个装满披萨的盒子，简直是改变命运的事。”保持社区无熊是一项“集体训练工作”，谢尔曼补充道。“你们必须步调一致，因为如果一个人院子里留了大量好东西，熊很可能想，‘我应该去别家院子看看。’”戈登说，他们在处理垃圾时“高度警惕”。“我们甚至不用自家垃圾桶。我一周几次把垃圾拖到办公室。”他们还保持门窗紧闭，从不将食物留在车内。它们不是泰迪熊，它们依然是野生动物——威尔逊·谢尔曼。这对夫妇表示，他们从未与到访家中的熊有过负面接触。马丁内斯曾因意外让车库门开着，发现纳皮在里面。“我们互相吓了一跳，”他说。“我慢慢后退，因为你永远不想困住熊。”他说，她从车库出来，然后自顾自地走了。更多类似内容：
为什么灰熊需要专属徒步小径
看到熊时该怎么做
德国浣熊泛滥的真实故事
谢尔曼说，像马丁内斯和戈登这样的社交媒体账号以及家庭监控摄像头，让人们“将熊视为个体，并深入了解它们的生活”。但他也有些保留意见。“总有迪士尼化的风险，即描绘出过于可爱的画面。它们不是泰迪熊，它们依然是野生动物。”谢尔曼警告说，熊和人类之间不应变得过于亲近，这一点很重要。“爱熊的一部分是建立健康的界限，并在它们不可避免地穿越我们社区时，为它们创造成功条件，”他说。通过他们专门记录熊的Instagram账号@poolbearlife，戈登和马丁内斯希望提高人们对如何在熊周围安全行事以及如何减少不必要遭遇的意识。他们强调，他们与黑熊的关系

这未必是放之四海而皆准的做法。“这对我们有效，对我们生活的地方有效，”戈登说。“关键在于找到与野生动物共存的平衡点，我们如何共同繁荣？”马丁内斯说。“我们住在这里，熊也住在这里。我们不希望它们去任何地方。”——如需获取关键气候新闻和充满希望的最新进展，请订阅《未来地球》时事通讯，而《要点清单》每周两次为您精选专题和见解。欲了解更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境和健康故事，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。地球 野生动物 自然与户外 环境 热浪 专题 熊

readings.title: Trump’s new mass deportation target
body: Today, Explained newsletter Trump’s new mass deportation target The Trump administration is going after Haitian immigrants after ending deportation protections. by Cameron Peters Aug 28, 2026, 9:20 PM UTC Gift Haitian immigrants at a protest in Salisbury, Maryland, on August 26, 2026. Dominic Gwinn/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Cameron Peters is a staff editor at Vox. This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here . After ending legal protections for 350,000 Haitians living in the United States, the Trump administration is ramping up its efforts to deport them back to a country engulfed in violence — and bragging about it. “Those with terminated TPS are in our nation Illegally,” the Department of Homeland Security X account posted on Thursday evening , alongside a video of chained Haitian immigrants set to cheery music. “They have two options: LEAVE IMMEDIATELY or be DEPORTED.” Temporary protected status (TPS) is extended to immigrants for whom conflict, natural disaster, or another catastrophe means returning home would be unsafe, and Haiti certainly qualifies: The island nation has been in crisis since its president was assassinated in 2021, with armed gangs controlling most of the capital city; earlier this week, dozens were killed and kidnapped near the capital. Despite all that, the administration first attempted to end TPS protections for Haitians living in the US last year, and succeeded after the Supreme Court gave its blessing in June. Now, it’s sending them back to a country where the State Department warns Americans not to travel “for any reason” because of “crime, terrorism, kidnapping, unrest, and limited health care.” On Thursday, that effort included a deportation flight carrying families with young children born in the US . Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. Haitian immigrants in the US aren’t the only people whom Immigrations and Customs Enforcement is targeting more aggressively. According to immigration data released this week by the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA, ICE arrested a record number of people in two consecutive months this summer: first 43,000 in June, then nearly 50,000 last month. As arrests surge, who’s being targeted is changing, too. More and more ICE arrestees don’t have a criminal record; in July, immigrants with only civil immigration violations made up a majority of arrests. Often, they also have active immigration cases pursuing asylum, a green card, or some other legal status, as the Seattle Times reported this week . Overall, ICE detentions are also rising again, though they’re still lower than they were at the start of the year. The pace of arrests reflects ICE’s growing size — 29,000 employees in June, according to the New York Times , compared to 21,000 in January 2025 — as well as its glut of cash after Trump’s reconciliation bill forked over $75 billion to the agency last year. Nonetheless, the agency still wants more: As the New York Times reported in July, its internal target for arrests is 2,000 per day . That would mean a record of at least 60,000 people per month, the majority likely guilty of no crime at all. ➨ Shop local. With food getting recalled left and right for all kinds of dire reasons (both related to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and not), farmers markets are getting more attention as an option for leafy greens that won’t leave you in crisis. But how do small farms pull it off, and how much of a difference does it make? The Vox video team headed to Camarillo, California , to investigate. Did you know… that three words might be all that’s standing between us and autonomous killer robots? As my colleague Kylie Jones explains , it’s the semantic difference between “meaningful human control” and “appropriate human judgment,” which is the Pentagon’s current standard. Today’s trivia: In which athletic conference does Georgia Tech compete? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword . Look for the answer in Monday’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday, we asked you which city serves as the headquarters of the National Collegiate Athletic Association. That would be Indianapolis. 在结束对居住在美国的35万海地移民的法律保护后，特朗普政府正加大力度将他们驱逐回一个深陷暴力的国家——并对此大肆吹嘘。“那些被终止临时保护身份的人在我国属非法居留，”国土安全部X账号周四晚间发文称，并附上一段海地移民被锁链束缚、配以欢快音乐的视频。“他们有两个选择：立即离开或被驱逐出境。”临时保护身份（TPS）适用于因冲突、自然灾害或其他灾难而返回本国不安全的移民，而海地无疑符合条件：自2021年总统遇刺以来，这个岛国一直处于危机之中，武装帮派控制着首都大部分地区；本周早些时候，首都附近有数十人被杀害或绑架。尽管如此，政府去年首次试图终止居住在美国的海地移民的TPS保护，并在6月获得最高法院批准后取得成功。现在，它正将他们送回一个国务院警告美国人“无论出于何种原因”都不要前往的国家，因为那里存在“犯罪、恐怖主义、绑架、动荡和有限的医疗资源”。周四，这一努力包括一架载有在美国出生的年幼子女家庭的驱逐航班。
