readings.title: Inside Earth's biggest telescope
body: 15 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Richard Fisher In Chile's Atacama Desert, the biggest telescope ever built is taking shape – and it could radically change our view of the Universe. Over the past 200 years, telescopes have got ever-bigger – which has posed a conundrum about what to call them. Some are named after eminent astronomers. Others after their location. But many get their titles from their sheer size. The astronomer William Herschel set the trend in the 18th Century with his Great Forty-Foot Telescope. And today, there's the Southern African Large Telescope , Spain's Gran Telescopio Canarias , and the Large Binocular Telescope in Arizona, to name a few. But what do you call a telescope that's bigger than large? For the scientists and engineers of the Paranal observatory in Chile's Atacama desert, the answer is simple: a process you might call "nominative magnification". In the 1990s, they needed a title for a particularly whopping telescope, which combined several individual instruments into one virtual mega-mirror. They scratched their heads for a while, and decided to name it the Very Large Telescope (VLT) . Now the same astronomers are going even more superlative, building a facility on a second Chilean mountain that will become Earth's biggest eye on the stars. Its name? Naturally, they're calling it the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) . And they are not kidding about the size: the ELT's dome is 80m tall (260ft), and the mirror inside is 39m wide (128ft). With an outer structure due to be completed in 2027, the organisation behind it – a consortium of 16 member states called the European Southern Observatory (Eso) – hope it will be peering into the cosmos by 2030. It's proven to be an enormous engineering challenge too, requiring tens of thousands of tonnes of concrete and steel, and 798 precisely engineered mirror segments , to be shipped to the top of an uninhabited mountain in the desert. Why build such a massive telescope in such a harsh and remote location? To find out, the BBC visited the ELT site in Chile, and discovered an extremely big telescope poised to make extremely big discoveries. In fact, it might even make the biggest discovery of them all. From a distance, it's difficult to get a handle on the size of the ELT. Approaching its mountaintop perch on Cerro Armazones, it first appears as a dot of silver glistening beneath an empty blue sky. Apart from a few road signs and the occasional industrial mine, there is almost no imprint of human habitation in the Atacama Desert, so nothing to offer a sense of scale. All the construction materials must be transported for hours from the nearest city, piece by piece, and the engineers here work in shifts of eight long days and nights before travelling back to their homes, sometimes hundreds of miles away. Look east and there is only boundless wilderness – from some places, you can see as far as Argentina – and to the west, the Pacific Ocean, topped by a sea of inverted cloud. The Atacama is not a desert of sand, but of rough rock, volcanic peaks, and salt flats. In some locations, rain comes only a few times a century, or not at all. With so little moisture, a visitor finds themselves continually licking their dry lips. Dehydration is a real danger, the altitude makes some nauseous, and the thin, cloudless air means that Earth's nearest star will burn your skin faster than almost anywhere else on the planet . Yet within this unforgiving setting, one of the world's most advanced telescopes is gradually assembling. To appreciate how complicated a project the ELT is, you have to step inside. Within the retractable, rotating dome lies a complex lattice of steel beams and moving parts that will hold the giant mirror in place. After a while, the back of your neck begins to ache because you're so frequently gazing upwards. "It's a cathedral in terms of the size and scale," says Michael Booth, the on-site mechanical engineering lead for the ELT, who is accompanying the BBC on a tour of the site. However, "extremely large" does not mean lumbering, or imprecise. On the contrary, assembling the telescope has required extensive planning and minute accuracy, says Booth. "It's too big and too complicated for us to say, 'I hope it works.' It's not like, 'let's hit this button and see if it makes any big noises,'" he says. To illustrate his point, Booth points at removable, millimetre-wide "shim packs" between the giant beams. These are necessary for tiny structural adjustments as the telescope's massive concrete base shrinks over time. That concrete, when it was laid, needed to be extraordinarily flat, he says, to an accuracy of 1/3,600th of a degree, and to account for the Earth's curvature too. (When they were finished, the engineers used the excess wet concrete to make a basketball court on the mountainside, because it was too far to the nearest city to return it before it hardened.) To gather light that has travelled from distant stars and galaxies, and to account for the atmosphere's blurring effects, astronomers need the telescope to be incredibly stable; the slightest wobble will lead to a fuzzy image. "The thing that makes construction of a telescope like this so hard is that usually the bigger you get, the bigger your tolerances – like how much wiggle room you have. But for us, obviously, the light waves don't get bigger," explains Booth. "And so we have to build to the scale of a large commercial building but with the tolerances you find on an optical bench." It's not a static structure, either. During operation, the entire building will rotate to face in different directions, suspended on high-pressure oil. "We float the whole telescope, so it can move basically frictionlessly," says Booth. "It's like an air hockey table." This puck, however, weighs many thousands of tonnes. The ELT's record-breaking mirror, in the centre of the structure, will be assembled from 798 individual, removable hexagonal segments, delicately polished. But unlike your bathroom mirror, there's no protective glass to shield against scrapes or dents. "That's the hard part," says Booth. "Most of the time if something weighs 10 tonnes you can hit it with a hammer. We can't even scratch the surface of it." The mirror segments, shipped from Europe in containers, are currently stored in a warehouse nearby: But when they are placed inside the structure, they will join to form one big mirror that is 39m (128ft) wide : No operating optical-infrared ground telescope currently has a mirror this huge. By comparison, the ELT's little brother – the Very Large Telescope, around 20 kilometres (12 miles) away – is made up of four telescopes each with mirrors of only 8.2m (27ft) diameter (plus four small 1.8m (6ft) diameter auxiliary telescopes). Each has to work together to combine their light. The ELT mirror's size – and the fact that it can change shape in real-time to account for atmospheric turbulence – will allow astronomers to scrutinise many objects with higher resolution than currently possible. In other words, the mirror is a "bigger bucket to collect light", says Eso astronomer Mariya Lyubenova. There's a limit to the sharpness of the images that the current generation of telescopes can create, even space-based telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), currently orbiting the Sun (which incidentally, has a mirror that's only 6.5m (21ft) wide.) Elyar Sedaghati, an Eso staff astronomer at the Paranal observatory, explains why the ELT offers a step-change for astronomers. "I​magine if you have a car that's coming from very far away at night," he says. "The car has two headlights but when it's really far away you cannot distinguish them. You only see a single light. The closer it gets, at some point, you start to separate the two lights." It's the same with stars, but a giant mirror essentially brings such overlapping starlight closer to Earth, allowing astronomers to distinguish what's in the field of view. Therefore, the ELT promises advances right across astronomy and physics. "It's just so multifaceted. It will really push the boundary and push the needle at every possible astronomical subfield that you can think of," says Sedaghati. So for example, the ELT will follow up on discombobulating discoveries recently made by JWST about the distant, early Universe, by imaging very far, very old galaxies that have never been scrutinised before. "It will be really amazing when the ELT starts, because it has a higher angular resolution compared to the James Webb, so we can combine observations," says Sedaghati. A space telescope alone can show us a lot, but a space telescope and a ground telescope together make for a great team. Closer to home, astronomers hope the ELT will be sensitive enough to help them calculate the ages of our own galaxy's oldest stars. The hope is also to peer closer at the stars revolving around the galactic centre, says Lyubenova, which could reveal deviations from current gravitational theories. And in our own neighbourhood, the telescope will be able to track objects like the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS that passed through our Solar System recently. But the biggest prize of all? It could well be the discovery that would change everything: evidence of life beyond Earth. In the 21st Century, we have entered a new era in the search for aliens. Some observers have called it the " age of alien agnosticism ": a time when a growing number of serious scientists strongly believe a basic form of extraterrestrial life is close to showing itself, but cannot yet prove it – their evidence accumulating piece-by-piece . It was once assumed that the discovery of aliens would involve flying saucers, radio signals or Martian megastructures . But it's more likely that we'll spot a more basic form of life first, revealing itself slowly to telescopes. We've already had signs: a compelling recent example was the apparently organic chemicals detected on the exoplanet K2-18b : a tantalising hint of marine organisms. It could be just the beginning. If you talk to serious astronomers about aliens, most are cautious, burnt by hyperbolic media claims , and slightly ticked off that you're not asking them about more sober activities like cataloguing galaxies. But they don't totally discount the possibility. In a recent survey of astrobiologists, physicists and other scientists, almost 90% agreed that it's likely that basic extraterrestrial life exists in the Universe. The numbers in the survey were lower for complex or intelligent life (around 60%), but they were also far from zero. The cosmos, after all, is a big place. "As an astronomer that works in this field, you have to be very careful," says Sedaghati. He is doubtful of finding intelligent life within the same broad expanse of space and time as us. But something like microbes or algae? That's different. "If you think about the number of stars that are only in our own galaxy and the number of planets around that are around these stars, and the proportion of those planets that are in a zone where you could possibly have life… if you just look at the sheer numbers, the probability that life exists somewhere else in the galaxy it's, for me, extremely high. There must be life out there." The sticking point is: what will count as strong evidence? And that's where the ELT comes in. It's not possible to image an exoplanet and see an alien waving back; it's not even possible to image landmasses. But we can study their habitability in other ways. For example, astronomers can infer whether a planet is rocky or gaseous. To do this, "we observe very tiny deviations in the wobble of a star", explains Lyubenova. This reveals the otherwise invisible nearby planet's gravitational effect, which in turn allows a calculation of its mass. Gas giants tend to have higher mass than rocky planets. Crucially, the ELT will be able to measure the masses of smaller, lower mass worlds than currently possible, she says, significantly expanding the candidates for hosting alien life. Astronomers can also analyse the constituents of exoplanet atmospheres, via the light spectrum of the starlight that occasionally passes through them on its way to Earth. "Each chemical element has its own imprint in the spectrum. It's like a fingerprint," says Lyubenova. So if an alien bacteria or some form of strange algae is belching out organic gases, it could show up. At the moment, it's difficult to study exoplanet atmospheres in the habitable zone of other solar systems, because such worlds are too close to the star. Like when you're dazzled by a car headlight, you can't see who is at the wheel. Claims about biosignatures on K2-18b in 2025 were controversial, because as well as disagreements about whether the detected gases are organic, the planet is also right at the edge of possible habitability. The ELT, however, could explore many more candidate worlds. In short, within as little as a decade, it is here – deep in the Chilean desert – that we may finally gain the evidence that aliens are out there, posing existential questions about our position in the cosmos. The age of alien uncertainty would end: we would finally realise that we are no longer alone. More like this: • The hotel where astronomers live like James Bond spies • The light disturbing a dark zone full of telescopes • The spacewalk that saved Hubble What comes after that is unknown. But already, astronomers have their eye on the next telescopes – which could be even bigger. "We are already thinking about other ways of pushing the boundary," says Sedaghati. For example, there are ideas like building lots of telescopes, kilometres apart, and connecting them to make a mega-telescope. In principle, if the existing Very Large Telescope was connected to a new telescope on another mountain-top via an "optical bridge" it would significantly boost its abilities, says Sedaghati. In the more distant future, people have talked about sending a space telescope beyond our Solar System's most distant planets so that we can use the Sun – and the fact its mass bends distant starlight – as a "gravitational lens". Essentially, the telescope would be the size of the Solar System. "This way you would actually not just image a planet around another star – an Earth-sized planet – but you would even be able to map the surface of it," says Sedaghati. "You would be able to tell more or less, where is oceans, where is land? These ideas are out there but it's just our technology needs to catch up." It begs the question: what do you call these behemoths if "extremely large" is already taken? A couple of decades ago, Eso was already considering whether to build the "Overwhelmingly Large Telescope". But a clue might come from an XKCD cartoon that jokes where they could go next: "oppressively colossal" is one option, or perhaps "mind-numbingly vast". For now though, astronomers wait. They know that by the 2030s, a cathedral to human curiosity will finally be peering into the cosmos. What they don't know yet is what it will find. -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.  For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . 15小时前 分享 保存 设为Google偏好 Richard Fisher 在智利的阿塔卡马沙漠，有史以来最大的望远镜正在成形——它可能彻底改变我们对宇宙的看法。过去200年间，望远镜变得越来越大——这引发了一个关于如何命名它们的难题。有些以著名天文学家命名，有些以所在地命名，但许多则根据其巨大尺寸得名。天文学家威廉·赫歇尔在18世纪开创了这一趋势，用他的“四十英尺大望远镜”树立了典范。如今，有南非大望远镜、西班牙加那利大望远镜、亚利桑那州的大双筒望远镜等。但你会如何称呼一个比“大”还大的望远镜呢？对于智利阿塔卡马沙漠帕拉纳尔天文台的科学家和工程师来说，答案很简单：一个你或许可以称之为“命名放大”的过程。在1990年代，他们需要为一个特别庞大的望远镜命名，该望远镜将多个独立仪器组合成一个虚拟的巨型镜面。他们挠头思考了一阵，决定将其命名为“甚大望远镜”（VLT）。现在，同一批天文学家正追求更高程度的极致，在智利的第二座山上建造设施，它将变成地球望向星辰的最大之眼。它的名字？自然，他们称之为“极大望远镜”（ELT）。他们对尺寸绝非儿戏：ELT的圆顶高80米（260英尺），内部镜面宽39米（128英尺）。外部结构预计于2027年完工，背后的组织——一个由16个成员国组成的联盟，称为欧洲南方天文台（Eso）——希望它能在2030年前开始凝视宇宙。这已被证明是一项巨大的工程挑战，需要数万吨混凝土和钢材，以及798块精密设计的镜片段，运送到沙漠中一座无人居住的山顶。为什么要在如此严酷偏远的地点建造这样一座巨型望远镜？为了解答这个问题，BBC探访了智利的ELT站点，发现了一座即将带来极大发现的极大望远镜。事实上，它甚至可能做出所有发现中最重要的那一个。从远处看，很难把握ELT的规模。靠近它在阿马索内斯山山顶的栖息地时，它最初只是空旷蓝天下闪烁的一个银色小点。除了少数路标和偶尔的工业矿场，阿塔卡马沙漠几乎没有任何人类居住的痕迹，所以没有参照物来提供尺度感。所有建筑材料必须从最近的城市花费数小时逐一运输，这里的工程师轮班工作，每次长达八天八夜，然后才返回他们的住处。

有些地方，甚至远在数百英里之外。向东望去，只有无边的荒野——从某些地点，你可以一直看到阿根廷——而西边是太平洋，上面覆盖着一片倒置的云海。阿塔卡马不是沙子的沙漠，而是粗糙岩石、火山峰和盐滩的沙漠。在某些地区，雨水一个世纪只降临几次，或者根本不降。由于水分如此稀少，来访者会发现自己不停地舔着干裂的嘴唇。脱水是真正的危险，高海拔让一些人感到恶心，而稀薄、无云的空气意味着，地球最近的恒星会比其他任何地方更快地灼伤你的皮肤。然而，在这片严酷的环境中，世界上最先进的望远镜之一正在逐步组装起来。

要理解ELT（极大望远镜）项目有多么复杂，你必须走进内部。在可伸缩、旋转的圆顶内，是一个由钢梁和活动部件组成的复杂网状结构，它将固定巨大的镜面。过了一会儿，你的后颈开始酸痛，因为你频繁地抬头仰望。“就其尺寸和规模而言，它就像一座大教堂，”ELT现场机械工程负责人迈克尔·布斯说，他正陪同BBC参观现场。然而，“极大”并不意味着笨重或不够精确。相反，组装这台望远镜需要广泛的规划和极高的精度，布斯说。“它太大、太复杂了，我们不能说‘我希望它能行’。它不是‘让我们按这个按钮，看看会不会发出什么大动静’那种事，”他说。为了说明他的观点，布斯指着巨梁之间可拆卸、毫米宽的“垫片组”。这些是必要的，用于随着望远镜巨大的混凝土底座随时间收缩而进行微小的结构调整。他说，铺设这些混凝土时，需要异常平整，精度达到1/3600度，并且还要考虑地球的曲率。（当他们完工时，工程师们用多余的湿混凝土在山腰上建了一个篮球场，因为距离最近的城市太远，无法在混凝土硬化前送回。）为了收集来自遥远恒星和星系的光，并消除大气模糊效应，天文学家需要望远镜极其稳定；最轻微的晃动都会导致图像模糊。“建造这样一台望远镜之所以如此困难，是因为通常你做得越大，你的公差就越大——比如你有多少活动余地。但对我们来说，显然，光波不会变大，”布斯解释说。“所以我们必须以大型商业建筑的规模来建造，但精度要求却要像光学实验台那样。”它也不是一个静态结构。在运行期间，

##段落  
整个建筑将悬浮在高压油上，旋转以面向不同方向。“我们让整个望远镜浮起来，这样它几乎可以无摩擦地移动，”布斯说，“就像空气曲棍球台一样。”然而，这个“圆盘”重达数千吨。ELT创纪录的镜面位于结构中心，将由798块独立、可拆卸的六边形片段组装而成，经过精细抛光。但与浴室镜子不同，它没有保护玻璃来抵御刮擦或凹痕。“这是最难的部分，”布斯说，“大多数时候，如果某物重10吨，你可以用锤子敲它，但我们连它的表面都不能划伤。”镜面片段从欧洲用集装箱运来，目前存放在附近的仓库中：但当它们被安置到结构内时，将拼接成一面宽达39米（128英尺）的大镜子：目前运行中的光学红外地面望远镜没有一面镜子有这么大。相比之下，ELT的“小兄弟”——甚大望远镜（距离约20公里/12英里）——由四台望远镜组成，每台镜面直径仅为8.2米（27英尺），外加四台直径1.8米（6英尺）的辅助望远镜。每台必须协同工作以合并它们的光线。ELT镜面的尺寸——以及它能实时变形以应对大气湍流的事实——将使天文学家能以比目前更高的分辨率仔细观测许多天体。换句话说，这面镜子是一个“更大的收集光线的桶”，ESO天文学家玛丽亚·柳贝诺娃说。当前一代望远镜（甚至包括目前在绕太阳运行、镜面仅6.5米/21英尺宽的詹姆斯·韦伯太空望远镜（JWST））所能产生的图像清晰度存在极限。ESO帕拉纳尔天文台的工作人员天文学家埃利亚尔·塞达加蒂解释了ELT如何为天文学家带来阶跃式变化。“想象一下，夜晚有一辆车从很远的地方驶来，”他说，“车有两个前灯，但当它真的很远时，你无法区分它们，只能看到一个光点。当它靠近时，在某个点，你开始分辨出两个灯光。”恒星也是如此，但一面巨大的镜子本质上将这种重叠的星光“拉近”到地球，使天文学家能分辨视野中的物体。因此，ELT有望推动整个天文学和物理学领域的进步。“它实在太多元化了。它将真正推动边界，在你能想到的每一个天文学子领域都推动进展，”塞达加蒂说。例如，ELT将通过对极远、极早期宇宙进行成像，跟进JWST最近关于遥远早期宇宙的令人困惑的发现。

那些从未被仔细审视过的古老星系。“当ELT启动时，那将是真正令人惊叹的时刻，因为它比詹姆斯·韦布有更高的角分辨率，所以我们可以结合观测，”塞达加提说。单独一台太空望远镜能向我们展示很多，但太空望远镜和地面望远镜结合起来会组成一个伟大的团队。在离地球更近的地方，天文学家希望ELT足够灵敏，能帮助他们计算出我们银河系中最古老恒星的年龄。柳贝诺娃说，还希望能更近距离地观测围绕银河系中心旋转的恒星，这可能揭示出当前引力理论的偏差。而在我们的邻近区域，这台望远镜将能追踪像最近穿过太阳系的星际彗星3I/ATLAS这样的天体。但最大的收获是什么？很可能是那种能改变一切的发现：地球以外存在生命的证据。在21世纪，我们已进入寻找外星人的新时代。一些观察者称之为“外星人不可知论时代”：在这个时代，越来越多严肃的科学家坚信某种基础形式的地外生命即将显现，但尚无法证明——他们的证据正在一点一点积累。曾几何时，人们以为发现外星人会涉及飞碟、无线电信号或火星巨型结构。但更有可能的是，我们首先会发现一种更基础的生命形式，它通过望远镜慢慢显露出来。我们已经有了迹象：一个令人信服的近期例子是在系外行星K2-18b上检测到的明显有机化学物质——这是海洋生物存在的诱人暗示。这可能只是开始。如果你和严肃的天文学家谈论外星人，大多数人会很谨慎，被夸张的媒体宣传所伤，并且因为你没问他们更务实的活动（如编目星系）而有点恼火。但他们并不完全排除这种可能性。在最近一项对天体生物学家、物理学家和其他科学家的调查中，近90%的人同意宇宙中很可能存在基础形式的地外生命。调查中，复杂或智能生命的数字较低（约60%），但也远非零。毕竟，宇宙是一个广阔的地方。“作为在这个领域工作的天文学家，你必须非常小心，”塞达加提说。他怀疑在与我们相同的广阔时空范围内能否找到智能生命。但像微生物或藻类这样的东西呢？那就不同了。“如果你想想仅我们银河系中恒星的数量，围绕这些恒星运行的行星数量，以及其中处于可能孕育生命区域的这些行星的比例……如果你只看纯数字，那么可能性——”

银河系中其他地方是否存在生命，在我看来，可能性极高。那里一定有生命存在。”症结在于：什么才算强有力的证据？这正是ELT发挥作用的地方。我们无法直接拍摄系外行星，看到外星人挥手；甚至无法成像其陆地。但我们可以通过其他方式研究它们的宜居性。例如，天文学家可以推断行星是岩石质还是气态的。要做到这一点，“我们观测恒星摆动中极其微小的偏差”，柳贝诺娃解释道。这揭示了原本不可见的邻近行星的引力效应，进而允许计算其质量。气态巨行星往往比岩石行星质量更大。关键在于，ELT将能测量比目前可能更小、更低质量的世界，她表示，这将显著扩大可能孕育外星生命的候选行星范围。天文学家还可以通过偶尔穿过系外行星大气层到达地球的星光光谱，分析其大气成分。“每种化学元素在光谱中都有独特的印记，就像指纹一样，”柳贝诺娃说。因此，如果外星细菌或某种奇异藻类排放出有机气体，就可能显现出来。目前，研究其他太阳系宜居带中的系外行星大气层很困难，因为这些世界离恒星太近。就像被汽车前灯晃到眼睛时，你看不清驾驶座上的人是谁。2025年关于K2-18b生物特征信号的声称引发争议，因为除了对探测到的气体是否为有机物的分歧外，该行星也恰好处于可能宜居的边缘。然而，ELT可以探索更多候选世界。简而言之，短短十年内，就在智利沙漠深处，我们或许最终能获得外星人存在的证据，这将对我们在宇宙中的位置提出根本性问题。外星不确定性的时代将终结：我们将最终意识到，我们不再孤独。更多类似内容：• 天文学家像詹姆斯·邦德间谍一样居住的酒店 • 干扰满是望远镜的暗区的光 • 拯救哈勃的太空行走。此后会发生什么尚不可知。但天文学家已经着眼于下一代望远镜——它们可能更大。“我们已经思考其他突破边界的方法，”塞达加提说。例如，有想法建造许多相距数公里的望远镜，并将其连接起来组成巨型望远镜。塞达加提表示，原则上，如果现有的甚大望远镜通过“光学桥”连接到另一座山顶的新望远镜，将显著增强其能力。在更遥远的未来，人们已经提出了一些构想。

我们曾讨论过将一台太空望远镜发射到太阳系最遥远行星之外，利用太阳——以及其质量弯曲遥远星光的事实——作为“引力透镜”。本质上，这台望远镜的规模将相当于整个太阳系。“这样一来，你不仅能直接拍摄到另一颗恒星周围的行星——比如地球大小的行星——甚至还能绘制其表面地图，”塞达加提说。“你大概能分辨出哪里是海洋，哪里是陆地？这些想法已经存在，只是我们的技术需要跟上。”这引出一个问题：如果“极大”已被占用，这些庞然大物该叫什么名字？几十年前，欧洲南方天文台已在考虑建造“压倒性大望远镜”。但线索可能来自一幅XKCD漫画，其中调侃下一步可用的名称：“压迫性巨大”是一种选择，或者也许是“令人麻木的浩瀚”。不过目前，天文学家们仍在等待。他们知道，到2030年代，一座人类好奇心的“大教堂”终将凝视宇宙。他们尚不知道的是，它会发现什么。——如果你喜欢这个故事，请订阅《要闻清单》通讯——每周两次精选特稿、视频和不容错过的新闻，直接发送至你的邮箱。欲了解更多BBC科学、技术、环境和健康故事，请关注我们的Facebook和Instagram账号。天文学望远镜太空宇宙物理特稿

readings.title: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do
body: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do

Ever have your hard work — including your successes — go unnoticed by your manager? Fixable , TED’s new podcast, is here to do just that — to fix the problems of everyday people who call in with their work woes.

In episode four , cohosts and top leadership coaches Frances Frei and Anne Morriss got to know Nai’a, a caller who struggled with receiving recognition after a major reorganization paired her with a new and preoccupied boss. Nai’a was going above and beyond to do her job well, but the lack of acknowledgement and encouragement — and even awareness — of her work was causing her to lose motivation.
Frances’s and Anne’s first piece of advice to Nai’a was simple: See the humanness of what’s going on — and of your manager.

“Sometimes the barrier to showing up as a great collaborator with your manager can be that there’s still some residual frustration about the situation,” Anne explained. “But that emotion is not going to be useful to you.”
Instead, they encouraged Nai’a to recognize the humanity of her manager and forgive them for making mistakes.
Frances and Anne also shared this strategy with her to practice: Choose curiosity over judgment.

Here’s how Frances put it: “You have a choice between judgment and curiosity, because both can’t exist at the same time. So if you have judgment about your manager, you can’t really be curious about their situation. And when you’re thinking of your manager as a person who’s got a lot of part-time jobs, how do we set them up for success?”

“The simplest expression of curiosity — which is truly a magical elixir in a workplace — is in the form of questions,” said Anne. For example, you could start by asking your manager what process works best for them to learn about your accomplishments and contributions. Or, you could focus on how you can make your meetings with them more productive by asking them, “How can our one-on-one time be of service to what we’re trying to achieve together?”

Another option: Be open about your concerns, and ask your manager what their vision of your success looks like. You could say something like, “Here’s my fear: I’m working really hard, and in this state of flux, I’m afraid that six months will go by and people are going to wonder whether or not I did a good job. So it’s just helpful for me to be clear — what is a good job and how can I help in getting that data for you?”

Across industries and across the world, many people are going through workplace reorganizations and other sweeping changes. And like Nai’a, it’s normal to feel anxious and stressed by what’s happening and to need to go through a readjustment period. Leading with questions — and seeing your boss as another human you’re collaborating with — can help you gain back some agency and autonomy.

“Try doing what you can, and marvel at how the other person changes as a result, as opposed to coming up with the list of how you would like the other person to change,” said Frances. “I think you’re going to be pleasantly surprised; that’s the beautiful part of this.”

No matter your job or business, you’ll find actionable advice on Fixable that can improve your workdays. In other episodes, learn how to overcome communication roadblocks, scale up your side project and lead more productive meetings. Plus: Click here for a chance to get your own work question answered on the show! Listen to Fixable now wherever you get your podcasts.
About the author Hayley Caldwell is a copywriter on the Audience Development team at TED.

感觉被老板忽视了吗？以下是你可采取的行动  
 2023年6月15日  
 /  
 海莉·考德威尔  
 Facebook  
 X  
 LinkedIn  
 Reddit

 Stocksy  

##段落
你是否曾有过这样的经历：你的辛勤工作——包括你的成功——被经理视而不见？TED的新播客《Fixable》正是为此而来——帮助那些带着职场烦恼来电的普通人解决问题。

##段落
在第四集中，联合主持人兼顶级领导力教练弗朗西斯·弗雷和安妮·莫里斯结识了来电者奈阿。在一次大规模重组后，她与一位新上任且心不在焉的老板搭档，努力争取认可。奈阿竭尽全力把工作做好，但缺乏认可、鼓励——甚至是对她工作的关注——让她逐渐失去动力。

##段落
弗朗西斯和安妮给奈阿的第一条建议很简单：看清事情的“人性面”——也看清你经理的“人性面”。

##段落
“有时，你无法与经理成为出色合作伙伴的障碍，可能是你对现状仍有一些残留的挫败感，”安妮解释道，“但那种情绪对你不会有帮助。”

##段落
相反，她们鼓励奈阿认识到经理的人性，并原谅他们犯错。

##段落
弗朗西斯和安妮还与奈阿分享了一个可以练习的策略：选择好奇，而非评判。

##段落
弗朗西斯是这样说的：“你可以在评判和好奇之间做选择，因为两者无法同时存在。如果你对经理有评判，你就无法真正对他们的处境感到好奇。而当你把经理看作一个身兼多职的人时，我们该如何为他们创造成功的条件？”

##段落
“好奇心的最简单表达——它确实是职场中的神奇灵药——就是以提问的形式呈现，”安妮说。例如，你可以先问问你的经理，什么流程最适合他们了解你的成就和贡献。或者，你可以专注于如何让与经理的会议更高效，问他们：“我们的一对一时间如何能为我们共同想要达成的目标服务？”

##段落
另一个选择：坦诚表达你的担忧，并询问经理他们对你成功的愿景是什么。你可以这样说：“我的担忧是：我非常努力地工作，在这种变动不定的状态下，我担心六个月过去后，人们会怀疑我是否做得好。所以，明确什么才是‘做得好’对我很有帮助——我该如何帮你获取这些信息？”

##段落
在全世界各行各业中，许多人都正在经历职场重组和其他大规模变革。和奈阿一样，对正在发生的事情感到焦虑和压力，并需要一个重新调整的过渡期，都是正常的。

带着问题去沟通——把上司视为与你协作的另一个普通人——可以帮助你重新获得一些主动权和自主性。  
“试着做你能做的事，然后惊奇地看到对方因此发生的变化，而不是列出一堆你希望对方改变的清单，”弗朗西斯说。“我想你会惊喜的；这就是这件事的美妙之处。”  
无论你从事什么工作或经营什么业务，你都能在《Fixable》节目中找到可操作的建议，改善你的工作日。在其他集数中，学习如何克服沟通障碍、扩展你的副业项目，以及主持更高效的会议。另外：点击这里，有机会在节目中提出你的工作问题并获得解答！现在就在你获取播客的任何平台收听《Fixable》吧。

readings.title: Is New York's cannabis business flying high?
body: 26 March 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Mike Wendling Five years after it was legalised in the state, cannabis is seemingly everywhere in New York. But, business owners say that many legitimate outlets are struggling – largely because of a thriving grey market, and the complicated legal status of the US cannabis industry. If you've recently visited New York, you've probably noticed something.  Advertisements outside bodegas display pictures of bright green flowers, higher-end dispensaries that resemble coffee bars or electronics shops welcome customers from all over the world, and then of course there's the smell – so seemingly omnipresent that even US Open tennis players have complained .  Weed is everywhere. From the outside it looks like a free-for-all, one that is drawing scepticism even from voices broadly supportive of the aims of the legalisation – including reducing harm and boosting tax revenue. Social media is rife with complaints (typical comments include "New York could not have screwed up legal weed any worse!") and for years the local press has been chronicling the rise of the "weed bodega" – typically a corner store selling products of dubious provenance. Across the country, weed consumption has increased – though studies indicate  that the rate of young people using has gradually declined since the turn of the century.  Things may have come to a head recently when the  New York Times , once a legal weed supporter, published an editorial headlined: "Marijuana Is Everywhere. That's a Problem." The newspaper now argues that "marijuana is causing more harm than predicted" and calls for tighter regulation.  But this new green rush is not as straightforward as it seems. Business owners say that public perceptions have been sullied by illegal operators, and that many above-board businesses are struggling – largely because of the incredibly complicated legal status of the US cannabis industry.  "At first glance, New York's cannabis industry appears to be booming," says Jayson Tantalo, a cannabis businessman and vice president of operations for the New York Cannabis Retail Association. "But that perception was initially driven by an oversaturation of illicit operators.  "These shops often presented themselves as legitimate, creating a misleading sense of scale and economic success," he says.  New York state legalised recreational use of cannabis five years ago this month . But legal wrangling and slow issuing of licenses hampered initial growth, while sales in other states such as California were racing ahead.   The bottleneck was so restrictive that some growers in New York complained that their crops were going to waste because of the lack of retail sales outlets. Meanwhile hundreds of those shady outlets sprang up, particularly in New York City.  Those wild days may be coming to an end. State authorities are starting to crack down on illegal operators, and police have been given power to immediately shut shops without a licence. And more legal businesses are being set up to address pent-up demand.  "It was really out of control," says Vlad Bautista, co-founder of Happy Munkey, a cannabis retailer in the Inwood neighbourhood of Manhattan.  "It made a little dent," he says of recent enforcement efforts. "But there’s still a long way to go." CRB Monitor, a firm that researches the cannabis industry, counts more than 2,000 active cannabis business licenses across the state – including retailers, wholesalers, growers and other types of cannabis companies – with another nearly 5,000 applications in the pipeline.  The effects can be seen far from Manhattan with weed shops popping up all across a state that is roughly the size of England.  Jayson Tantalo owns one of them. He was involved in the weed business long before it was legal. "What started as survival evolved into deep expertise in the industry," he says. He and his wife Britni set up their Flower City Dispensary retail business in Victor, a suburban community in western New York state with a population of about 16,000.  Tantalo says that while the industry is "highly visible and normalised" across the state, only a small percentage of legal operators have captured large shares of the market.  "Growth exists, but it's constrained, uneven, and still stabilising," he says.  New York's growing pains are just one example of the extraordinarily complicated legal status of cannabis that has caused confusion across the country - for businesses, customers and the public.  The patchwork legal regime around the industry is a product of cannabis's long strange trip from respectability to contraband and back again. George Washington, the first US president, famously grew hemp crops at his estate.   But waves of restrictions followed, culminating in a 1970 law that deemed marijuana a Schedule I drug – the most restrictive category.  Despite the US government's war on drugs, there has always been a significant movement calling for looser regulations on cannabis. That movement gradually became more mainstream in the early years of this century.  Support for legalising cannabis first cracked 50% of Americans in 2013, according to polling firm Gallup, and that figure has since risen to more than two-thirds today.  But instead of blanket legalisation, reforms came in piecemeal fashion, on the state and sometimes even the local level, creating a fragmented state-by-state market.  To top it off, weed remains illegal under federal law – thousands of people still get arrested each year for marijuana possession and related crimes.  This legal patchwork results in some bizarre consequences. A road-tripper heading west from New York would pass through Pennsylvania, where recreational use of marijuana is illegal, and then into Ohio, where it was legalised by a 2023 referendum. If they continued along Interstate 80 they would eventually get to Indiana (where weed is illegal), Illinois (legal), and Iowa (illegal) – and so on.  That's confusing in itself. But another legal loophole has opened the door for all sorts of grey-market and online businesses, effectively making cannabis accessible to nearly everyone in the country.  The 2018 Farm Bill legalised hemp with a relatively low level of tetrahydrocannabinol or THC – the chemical that gets cannabis users high.  Hemp contains CBD – a chemical that doesn’t produce the high of THC but has some health benefits. A glut of CBD ensued. And in a lab, CBD can be converted into psychoactive THC.  "Entrepreneurs could say, 'this is just hemp', even if what they were producing was a highly intoxicating form of THC," says Chris Lindsay, vice president of policy and state advocacy for the American Trade Association for Cannabis and Hemp (ATACH), which represents licenced businesses.  Those products are sold online or in those weed bodegas – even in states that have not legalised marijuana.  Robin Goldstein, an economist at the University of California-Davis and co-author of the book Can Legal Weed Win?: The Blunt Realities of Cannabis Economics, estimates that just behind California, the second-biggest weed market is in Texas, despite the Lone Star state's blanket ban on recreational cannabis use.  Business owners like Jason Ambrosino, have become used to dealing with spiralling legal complexities.  Ambrosino is founder and chief executive of Veterans Holdings, a weed business based in Gloversville, New York, about three hours north of New York City. An army vet who was seriously injured in Iraq, he got into the cannabis industry after discovering that medical marijuana was effective in alleviating his pain. These days, he says his legal headaches include rules that make it impossible to branch out into neighbouring states or to obtain traditional sources of financing.  "There’s a million different ways to get institutional funding, but you can’t get any of those for cannabis because of federal law," he says.  Despite the headwinds, Ambrosino has managed to grow his business and now employs around 80 people, and is hopeful that the increased licences for legal shops in New York will mean more sales opportunities down the line.  Vlad Bautista, the Happy Munkey co-founder, roughly estimates that he spends 40% of his time complying with various regulations, and, in particular, he questions some of the rules around advertising and tax law.  "If you own a cannabis business, you have much stricter advertising regulations than companies selling alcohol, cigarettes or gambling," he says. "You're stuck in the stone age, handing out flyers on the street." A buzz ran through the industry in December of last year, when President Trump signed an executive order which directed officials to accelerate efforts to reclassify marijuana to a less stringent category.  That might eventually give cannabis businesses some added profits – due to another federal law, weed companies aren't able to deduct all of their normal business expenses from their taxes. But businesspeople and experts aren't holding their breath for a practical impact any time soon.  "It's smoke and mirrors," says Naomi Granger, founder and chief executive of the National Association of Cannabis Accounting and Tax Professionals, who says some headlines heralding a new dawn for the cannabis industry have been somewhat misleading.  Some industry insiders say uncertainty is part and parcel of a nascent industry.  Steve Kemmerling, founder and chief executive of CRB Monitor, notes that states that were earlier to legal weed – California and Colorado in the western US were among the first – experienced hiccups on the way to relative stability.  "In any new market you're going to have wild volatility and price swings, mergers and acquisitions, along with competitive businesses and people cutting corners," he says.  And in a buzzy industry perhaps it's not surprising to encounter businesspeople who seem hard wired for sunny-day thinking.  "I'm an optimist," says Vlad Bautista. "We live in a divided and polarised world where nobody agrees on everything, and when you look at public opinion, there's a majority of people who agree on legal cannabis." "We've made a ton of progress," he says, "but there's still a long way to go." 自该州合法化五年后，大麻在纽约似乎无处不在。但企业主表示，许多合法门店正陷入困境——主要是因为灰色市场猖獗，以及美国大麻行业复杂的法律地位。

##段落
如果你最近去过纽约，你可能会注意到一些现象。杂货店外的广告展示着亮绿色花朵的图片，类似咖啡吧或电子产品商店的高端药房迎接来自世界各地的顾客，当然还有那种气味——似乎无处不在，连美国网球公开赛的球员都抱怨过。大麻无处不在。

##段落
从表面看，这像是一场无序的狂欢，甚至引起了一些原本广泛支持合法化目标（包括减少危害和增加税收）的声音的质疑。社交媒体上充斥着抱怨（典型评论包括“纽约把合法大麻搞得一团糟！”），多年来当地媒体一直在报道“大麻杂货店”的兴起——通常是销售来源可疑产品的街角商店。

##段落
全国范围内，大麻消费量有所增加——尽管研究表明，自世纪之交以来，年轻人的使用率逐渐下降。事情可能最近达到了顶点，《纽约时报》——曾经是大麻合法化的支持者——发表了一篇题为“大麻无处不在。这是个问题”的社论。该报现在认为“大麻造成的危害比预期更大”，并呼吁加强监管。

##段落
但这场新的绿色热潮并非表面看起来那么简单。企业主表示，公众认知已被非法经营者玷污，许多合规企业正陷入困境——主要是因为美国大麻行业极其复杂的法律地位。

##段落
“乍一看，纽约的大麻行业似乎正在蓬勃发展，”大麻商人、纽约大麻零售协会运营副总裁杰森·坦塔洛说。“但这种认知最初是由非法运营者的过度饱和驱动的。”

##段落
“这些商店往往将自己伪装成合法经营，制造了一种关于规模和经济效益的误导性印象，”他说。

##段落
纽约州于五年前的这个月将娱乐用大麻合法化。但法律纠纷和许可证发放缓慢阻碍了初期增长，而加利福尼亚等其他州的销售则飞速发展。瓶颈如此严重，以至于一些纽约种植者抱怨他们的作物因缺乏零售销售渠道而浪费。与此同时，数百家那些可疑门店如雨后春笋般涌现，尤其是在

在纽约市，那些狂野的日子可能即将结束。州当局开始打击非法经营者，警方已获授权立即关闭无照商店。同时，更多合法企业正在设立，以满足被压抑的需求。“当时真的失控了，”曼哈顿因伍德社区大麻零售商Happy Munkey的联合创始人弗拉德·鲍蒂斯塔说。他谈到近期的执法努力时表示：“这起了一点作用，但还有很长的路要走。”研究大麻行业的公司CRB Monitor统计，全州有超过2000个活跃的大麻商业许可证——包括零售商、批发商、种植者及其他类型的大麻公司——另有近5000份申请正在审批中。这种影响远不止曼哈顿，大麻店遍布全州，该州面积大致相当于英格兰。杰森·坦塔洛是其中一家店的老板。他在大麻合法化之前很久就涉足这一行业。“最初是为了生存，后来演变成对行业的深厚专业了解，”他说。他和妻子布里特尼在纽约州西部维克多镇（人口约16000人）开设了他们的Flower City Dispensary零售业务。坦塔洛表示，尽管该行业在全州“高度可见且已正常化”，但只有少数合法经营者占据了较大的市场份额。“增长存在，但受限、不均衡，且仍在稳定过程中，”他说。纽约的成长烦恼只是大麻极其复杂法律地位的一个例子，这种复杂性在全国范围内给企业、顾客和公众造成了困惑。围绕该行业的零散法律体系，是大麻从体面到违禁品再回归的漫长奇异旅程的产物。美国第一任总统乔治·华盛顿曾在其庄园种植大麻，这是众所周知的事。但随后限制浪潮接踵而至，最终在1970年的一部法律中将大麻列为第一类管制药物——这是最严格的类别。尽管美国政府发动了“毒品战争”，但一直有重要运动呼吁放宽对大麻的管制。本世纪初，这一运动逐渐走向主流。根据民调公司盖洛普的数据，2013年支持大麻合法化的美国人比例首次突破50%，如今这一数字已升至三分之二以上。但改革并非全面合法化，而是在州甚至地方层面零敲碎打地进行，形成了各州割裂的市场。更糟的是，大麻在联邦法律下仍然非法——每年仍有数千人因持有大麻及相关犯罪被捕。这种法律拼凑局面……

工作成果导致了一些奇怪的后果。从纽约向西行驶的公路旅行者会经过宾夕法尼亚州，那里娱乐性使用大麻是非法的，然后进入俄亥俄州，2023年的公投使其合法化。如果他们继续沿着80号州际公路行驶，最终会到达印第安纳州（大麻非法）、伊利诺伊州（合法）和爱荷华州（非法），如此等等。这本身就令人困惑。但另一个法律漏洞为各种灰色市场和在线业务打开了大门，实际上使全国几乎所有人都能获得大麻。2018年的农业法案将四氢大麻酚（THC）含量相对较低的大麻合法化，THC是让大麻使用者产生兴奋感的化学物质。大麻含有CBD——一种不会产生THC那种兴奋感但具有某些健康益处的化学物质。随后出现了CBD过剩。在实验室里，CBD可以转化为具有精神活性的THC。“企业家可以说‘这只是大麻’，即使他们生产的是高度致醉形式的THC，”美国大麻与工业大麻贸易协会（ATACH）政策与州倡导副总裁克里斯·林赛说，该协会代表持牌企业。这些产品在网上或那些大麻便利店销售，甚至在未将大麻合法化的州也是如此。加州大学戴维斯分校的经济学家罗宾·戈尔茨坦是《合法大麻能赢吗？：大麻经济的直白现实》一书的合著者，他估计，仅次于加利福尼亚州，第二大麻市场是德克萨斯州，尽管孤星州全面禁止娱乐性大麻使用。像杰森·安布罗西诺这样的企业主已经习惯了应对日益复杂的法律问题。安布罗西诺是退伍军人控股公司的创始人兼首席执行官，这是一家位于纽约州格洛弗斯维尔的大麻企业，距离纽约市以北约三小时车程。作为一名在伊拉克受重伤的陆军退伍军人，他在发现医用大麻能有效缓解疼痛后进入了这一行业。他说，如今他的法律麻烦包括一些规则，这些规则使他无法扩展到邻近州或获得传统融资来源。“有无数种方式可以获得机构资金，但由于联邦法律，你无法为大麻行业获得任何这些资金，”他说。尽管面临逆风，安布罗西诺还是设法扩大了业务，现在雇佣了大约80人，并希望纽约州增加合法商店的许可证意味着未来会有更多销售机会。Happy Munkey联合创始人弗拉德·鲍蒂斯塔粗略估计，他花费40%的时间来遵守各种法规，尤其是对广告和税法的一些规则提出质疑。“如果你拥有一家大麻店……”

##段落  
他说：“在商业领域，你面临的广告监管比销售酒精、香烟或赌博的公司严格得多。你就像困在石器时代，只能在街上发传单。”去年12月，行业里掀起了一阵热潮，当时特朗普总统签署了一项行政命令，指示官员加快将大麻重新归类到更宽松类别的进程。这可能最终会给大麻企业带来一些额外利润——因为另一项联邦法律，大麻公司目前无法从税收中扣除所有正常业务开支。但商界人士和专家们并不急于期待短期内产生实际影响。全国大麻会计与税务专业人士协会创始人兼首席执行官娜奥米·格兰杰表示：“这不过是烟雾弹。”她说，一些宣称大麻行业迎来新曙光的头条新闻有些误导性。一些业内人士表示，不确定性是这个新兴行业的一部分。CRB Monitor创始人兼首席执行官史蒂夫·凯默林指出，较早合法化大麻的州——美国西部的加利福尼亚州和科罗拉多州是最早的一批——在走向相对稳定的过程中也经历了波折。他说：“在任何新市场中，你都会遇到剧烈的波动和价格起伏、并购交易，以及竞争激烈的企业和偷工减料的行为。”而在一个热闹非凡的行业里，遇到似乎天生就乐观的商人也许并不令人意外。弗拉德·鲍蒂斯塔说：“我是个乐观主义者。我们生活在一个分裂且两极分化的世界里，没有人在所有事情上都能达成一致，但当你看看民意，大多数人都赞同大麻合法化。”他说：“我们已经取得了很大的进展，但还有很长的路要走。”如需药物成瘾方面的支持，请访问BBC Action Line。——如需获取面向董事会及其他领域的全球见解和专家分析，请订阅《商业世界》时事通讯，而《必读清单》则会提供精心挑选的特稿和洞察。如需了解更多商业及更广泛领域的资讯，请在LinkedIn上关注我们。商业 药物 特稿

readings.title: The weird coalition taking on Flock
body: Today, Explained newsletter The weird coalition taking on Flock Liberals and conservatives can agree to hate Flock cameras. Passionately. by Caitlin Dewey Aug 27, 2026, 9:10 PM UTC Gift A Flock camera photographed in Costa Mesa, California, on August 17, 2026. Paul Bersebach/Getty Images Caitlin Dewey is a senior writer and editor at Vox, where she helms the Today, Explained newsletter. This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here . I passed five Flock cameras on my drive to work today, entirely without realizing it. The AI-powered license plate readers have metastasized on light poles and roadside posts across the country over the past few years, building a vast national database of vehicle movements that law enforcement agencies can access with few restrictions. What are they doing with all that data? Who has access, and for how long? We don’t have clear answers to these questions — and lawmakers on both the right and the left increasingly want them. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. Yesterday, Senate Republicans opened an inquiry into Flock’s data “collection, retention, and dissemination” practices — a first step that could eventually lead to federal regulation. State officials have also called for restrictions: The technology is “out of control,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said during a Wednesday press conference. It is one of maybe three times, I would hazard, that DeSantis and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders have agreed on anything. Earlier this month, the independent senator also warned that Flock knows when you’re going to the doctor or dropping your kid off at school, among other things. For many Americans, his warning was no exaggeration: There are now 120,000 Flock cameras on US roads. You can use the crowdsourced map DeFlock to check your area. As the existence of a crowdsourced anti-Flock map might attest…people really do not like these cameras. In Tennessee this month, one conservative county commissioner went so far as to call for the hanging of Flock’s CEO. Even data centers rarely attract that level of vitriol . But as with data centers, both sides can find something to hate here , the longtime tech reporter Jason Koebler recently told Vox. On the right, critics typically attack the cameras as government overreach: “‘This is invasive government. This is Big Brother. Don’t surveil me,’” Koebler paraphrased. On the left, critics frequently link the cameras to corporate surveillance, racist policing, the erosion of abortion rights, and immigration enforcement: “This protest is about more than license plate readers,” one progressive activist recently put it . “It’s about…mass surveillance as a tool for fascism and political persecution.” The issue has surfaced in midterm races in states including Florida , Ohio , and Michigan, where some candidates have sought to link their opponents — fairly or unfairly — to Flock. In Michigan, for instance, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed released a campaign video last week that suggested voters could “thank” his opponent for the proliferation of the cameras. That video includes footage from a hearing Rogers chaired in 2013, before Flock was even founded; Rogers has not publicly responded. Political responsibility for the cameras is complicated, of course: Flock typically inks its contracts with cities, counties, and local police departments, which state and national lawmakers don’t approve. But they could certainly limit the use of automated plate readers in other ways, like requiring warrants for accessing data, limiting how long information is saved, and banning the cameras near schools, churches, abortion clinics, and other sensitive places. ➨ Put your phone away. Clubs, bars, music venues, and other social spaces are increasingly hosting “phone-free” gatherings — an attempt to break free from the distraction and surveillance of our screens. These things are popping up everywhere, so chances are you can find one somewhere near you. But if not, it’s pretty easy to throw your own phone-free game night or book club, too. Did you know… that women experiencing cardiac arrest are 14 percent less likely than men to receive CPR? Bystanders are apparently less comfortable performing the procedure on people with breasts, which has prompted calls for better-endowed CPR training manikins. Today’s trivia: What city serves as the headquarters of the National Collegiate Athletic Association? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword . Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the stage name of the singer Paul David Hewson. That would be Bono, which is short for “Bono Vox” — a childhood nickname inspired by a Dublin hearing-aid shop. 凯特琳·杜威是Vox的高级撰稿人和编辑，负责《今日解释》通讯。本文发表于《今日解释》，这是一份每日通讯，帮助你理解当天最引人注目的新闻和故事。在此订阅。
今天开车上班的路上，我经过了五台Flock摄像头，完全没有意识到它们的存在。过去几年里，这种人工智能驱动的车牌识别设备已在全美的灯柱和路边立柱上迅速蔓延，构建起一个庞大的车辆行驶轨迹全国数据库，执法机构几乎不受限制地访问它。他们拿这些数据做什么？谁能访问，能访问多久？我们对这些问题没有明确答案——而左右两派的立法者越来越想要答案。

昨天，参议院共和党人对Flock的数据“收集、保留和传播”做法展开了调查——这是可能最终走向联邦监管的第一步。州官员也呼吁限制：这项技术“失控了”，佛罗里达州州长罗恩·德桑蒂斯在周三的新闻发布会上说。我敢说，这大概是德桑蒂斯和佛蒙特州参议员伯尼·桑德斯达成一致的仅有的三次之一。本月初，这位独立参议员也警告说，Flock知道你去看医生或送孩子上学的时机，以及其他种种。对许多美国人来说，他的警告并非夸大其词：目前美国道路上已有12万台Flock摄像头。你可以使用众包地图DeFlock来查看你所在地区的情况。
正如一张众包反Flock地图的存在所证明的那样……人们真的不喜欢这些摄像头。本月在田纳西州，一位保守派县委员甚至呼吁绞死Flock的首席执行官。即使是数据中心也很少招致这种程度的敌意。但正如数据中心一样，双方都能在这里找到值得讨厌的东西，资深科技记者杰森·科布勒最近告诉Vox。在右翼，批评者通常将这些摄像头攻击为政府越权：“‘这是侵入性的政府。这是老大哥。别监视我，’”科布勒转述道。在左翼，批评者经常将这些摄像头与企业监控、种族主义执法、堕胎权利的侵蚀以及移民执法联系起来：“这场抗议是关于……”

这不仅仅是车牌识别摄像头的问题，”一位进步派活动人士最近表示，“这关乎……作为法西斯主义和政治迫害工具的大规模监控。”这一问题已在佛罗里达州、俄亥俄州和密歇根州等地的中期选举中浮出水面，一些候选人试图将对手与Flock公司挂钩——无论公平与否。例如，在密歇根州，民主党参议员候选人阿卜杜勒·埃尔-赛义德上周发布了一段竞选视频，暗示选民可以“感谢”他的对手导致了这些摄像头的泛滥。该视频包含罗杰斯在2013年主持的一场听证会的画面，当时Flock甚至尚未成立；罗杰斯尚未公开回应。当然，摄像头的政治责任很复杂：Flock通常与城市、县和当地警察部门签订合同，而这些并不需要州或国家立法者的批准。但他们肯定可以通过其他方式限制自动车牌识别器的使用，例如要求获取数据必须持有搜查令、限制信息保存时间，以及禁止在学校、教堂、堕胎诊所和其他敏感场所附近安装摄像头。

readings.title: The secure retro tech that confounds hackers
body: 4 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Chris Baraniuk The fear of hacking has made some people turn to other forms of technology ignored by new generations of cyber criminals. You might not expect a world-renowned cyber security expert to rely on old, potentially vulnerable email software. But, for years, that's what Mikko Hyppönen did. Shunning mainstream options such as Hotmail and Gmail, he instead chose obsolete email software called Eudora. "I used to run it years after it was out of [technical] support," says Hyppönen, a Finnish computer security expert.   He preferred Eudora for various reasons, arguing it was "really superior in many ways". Although Eudora was far from perfectly secure , as people switched to newer email tools, Hyppönen realised that hackers were forgetting about Eudora. Hyppönen calls it "security by antiquity". Others use the phrase "security by obsolescence" and in both cases this means relying on an older technology or system since it may prove, somewhat counterintuitively, safer than more recent alternatives. While Hyppönen stresses that using the latest, fully patched and updated software is still "the optimum situation", there are specific cases where older tech could be preferable from a security standpoint. "The vast majority of attackers are criminals trying to make money and it doesn't make any sense for them to target systems being run by 50 people," he explains. Hyppönen isn't alone. The Irish Aviation Authority, for instance, recently decided to keep ground-based radio navigation beacons in use because supposedly the more modern satellite-based global positioning system (GPS) has proven so susceptible to jamming in recent years. "Security by antiquity" is, it turns out, a quiet way of beating cyber-criminals, hackers and enemy attackers. Matt Bishop, a computer scientist and professor emeritus at the University of California, Davis, has tested this principle, somewhat by accident. Back in the 1990s, he and his colleagues set up a system connected to the internet and deliberately left it accessible so that they could catch hackers and bots attempting to breach it. This is a common cyber-security research technique known as a honeypot – a kind of trap set up in carefully controlled conditions. But the team picked an older software version for their honeypot that had been upgraded multiple times since its release and, consequently, no hackers bothered to target it. "When we upgraded it to the new one, we had all the attacks we wanted," recalls Bishop. "I thought it was so amusing." This possibility of evading nefarious activity by sticking to old tech can take many forms. Both Bishop and Hyppönen say they have friends who refuse to get a smartphone. "One person I know [uses] a Nokia 9210," says Hyppönen, referring to a simple, "dumb" mobile phone first released 25 years ago. As technology has advanced, experts have often questioned whether the latest systems are actually more risky than older ones While hackers can't target it in quite the same way they might target a modern Android or iOS device, the phone's operating system, Symbian, does have some old, known vulnerabilities. The flipside is that "nobody's targeting them anymore", adds Hyppönen. Similarly, the Nokia could be more at risk from techniques that snoop on phone calls . But how many people will bother? It's a security trade-off. As technology has advanced, experts have often questioned whether the latest systems are actually more risky than older ones. During the late 1990s, Bishop wrote a speech in which he argued that computers were "considerably less secure than the paper systems we still use, and that are rapidly being replaced". Concerns about the shift from paper to digital technologies remain prevalent , especially when it comes to electronic voting systems . Some say electronic voting machines are desirable partly because they produce election results much more quickly than paper-based systems. That's not enough to sway others, though. "Voting is the bedrock of our democracy," says Hyppönen. "It's one of the last things I'd like to weaken in any way, especially if the benefits are so small." Militaries are also known for being reluctant to take chances. Even the world's most active militaries are known to occasionally rely on old technologies for reasons of reliability and security. "One thing I've seen in places like Ukraine is the use of paper maps, or laminated maps, and compasses," says Thomas Withington, associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a think tank. "You can't jam that." It's a kind of "analogue resilience", he adds. Jamming attacks hitting GPS-based navigation have forced some countries to make careful choices about which legacy technologies to retain, and which GPS alternatives to invest in, says Victor Tasiemski, a systems engineer at Overlook Systems Technologies, which works on navigation tech. That's exactly what happened in Ireland, where a programme to replace ground-based radio beacons has been slowed down in order to keep those beacons operating for longer. A spokeswoman for the Irish Aviation Authority told the Irish Times in June that the beacons were being retained "as part of a planned resilience strategy". Technologists who work with militaries are familiar with the challenge of designing systems that can link old and new technologies together. Stefan Kraus is co-founder and chief technical officer of Kraus Hamdani Aerospace, which has designed a drone-based communications platform that can connect military personnel to one another, no matter whether they are using older radios or newer ones. Military radio tech that has been around for decades is "tried, tested and secure", he says. "The US military isn't going away from that." Ransomware is what, for me, kept tape in business the past 10 to 15 years – Hugues Meyrath Tasiemski notes that one alternative to GPS-based navigation is eLoran, a radio-based navigation system that has its roots in military technology first developed during World War Two . With attacks targeting GPS systems, eLoran is arguably becoming increasingly desirable, says Tasiemski, because it uses a much more powerful signal and is therefore much trickier to jam: "Overpowering a one-megawatt transmitter is pretty hard." Robustness is not easy to replace. This applies in the world of data storage, too, where magnetic tape – invented during the 1950s – still plays a huge role today. Companies, research institutions and government agencies continue to store vast amounts of data on reels of tape. The technology has improved significantly since it first appeared, with data storage densities having increased exponentially over the decades . But the principle remains the same: spools of tape that hold information. The tape can be detached from computer systems, packaged, and transported to secure facilities, including difficult-to-breach underground caverns and repurposed mines . "Ransomware is what, for me, kept tape in business the past 10 to 15 years," says Hugues Meyrath, chief executive of Quantum, a company that specialises in data storage. An organisation locked out of its own computer systems may still be able to retrieve its most important data if staff have made good back-ups, for example on magnetic tape. Interest in magnetic tape is only increasing further today because the cost of random access memory (Ram), a form of computer memory that doesn't rely on tape, is skyrocketing . Meyrath says his company's clients use tape to store all kinds of data – from broadcasters' footage of baseball games to genomes mapped in detail by research facilities. More like this: •  Analogue technology can be frustrating – is that part of the appeal? •  Why analogue design still endures •  The people who hunt down old TVs Tape's security attributes stem partly from the fact that most people don't tend to interact with it at all. It's obscure, clunky, old-school tech. "One way to attack a system is to rig a set of USB sticks and throw them around a parking lot," says Bishop, referring to the likelihood that someone will eventually pick up one of the USB sticks and insert it into their computer – a simple way to perpetrate a hack. As he puts it: "You'll never see magnetic tape thrown around a parking lot." Experts who spoke to the BBC still recommend that people use the latest and most up-to-date technologies for everyday tasks, as it remains the safest approach. But it is worth acknowledging that "new" doesn't necessarily mean "best" in all scenarios. And knowing when and how to switch to older systems could become increasingly important, as cyber-attacks and other threats get more sophisticated. Withington points again to Ukraine, where Russia has interfered with satellite communications and where GPS navigation has succumbed to significant jamming . Nowhere is "analogue resilience" more prized. "What do people do," asks Withington, "if there's no access to the technology they take for granted?" -- For more insights, sign up to our Tech Decoded newsletter, where Lily Jamali and Thomas Germain break down the biggest stories of the tech world, and help you live a better digital life. 4天前 分享 保存 设为Google偏好 克里斯·巴拉纽克 对黑客攻击的恐惧使一些人转向了新一代网络犯罪分子所忽视的其他形式的技术。你可能不会想到一位世界知名的网络安全专家会依赖老旧、可能易受攻击的电子邮件软件。但多年来，米科·海波宁正是这样做的。他避开了Hotmail和Gmail等主流选项，转而选择了过时的电子邮件软件Eudora。“我在它停止技术支持多年后仍在使用它，”芬兰计算机安全专家海波宁说。他出于多种原因偏爱Eudora，认为它在“许多方面确实优越”。尽管Eudora远非完全安全，但随着人们转向更新的电子邮件工具，海波宁意识到黑客们正在遗忘Eudora。海波宁称之为“古旧安全”。其他人则用“过时安全”这一说法，两者都意味着依赖较旧的技术或系统，因为出乎意料的是，这可能比更新的替代品更安全。虽然海波宁强调使用最新、完全修补和更新的软件仍然是“最佳状态”，但在特定情况下，从安全角度来看，旧技术可能更可取。“绝大多数攻击者是为了赚钱的罪犯，他们针对只有50人使用的系统毫无意义，”他解释道。海波宁并非孤例。例如，爱尔兰航空管理局最近决定继续使用地面无线电导航信标，因为据称更现代的基于卫星的全球定位系统（GPS）近年来已被证明极易受到干扰。事实证明，“古旧安全”是一种悄然击败网络罪犯、黑客和敌方攻击者的方式。马特·毕晓普是加州大学戴维斯分校的计算机科学家和名誉教授，他在某种程度上偶然测试了这一原则。早在1990年代，他和同事们建立了一个连接到互联网的系统，并故意让其保持可访问状态，以便捕捉试图入侵的黑客和机器人。这是一种常见的网络安全研究技术，称为蜜罐——一种在严格控制条件下设置的陷阱。但团队为他们的蜜罐选择了较旧的软件版本，该版本自发布以来已多次升级，因此没有黑客费心去攻击它。“当我们升级到新版本时，我们得到了所有想要的攻击，”毕晓普回忆道。“我觉得这太有趣了。”这种通过坚持旧技术来逃避恶意活动的可能性可以采取多种形式。毕晓普和海波宁都说他们有朋友拒绝使用智能手机。“我认识的一个人用诺基亚9210，”海波宁说。

指的是一款25年前首次发布的简单“傻瓜”手机。随着技术的进步，专家们经常质疑最新系统是否实际上比旧系统风险更高。虽然黑客无法像攻击现代安卓或iOS设备那样直接攻击它，但这款手机的操作系统Symbian确实存在一些已知的旧漏洞。另一面是“没有人再针对它们了”，Hyppönen补充道。同样，诺基亚可能更容易受到窃听电话技术的影响。但有多少人会费心去攻击呢？这是一种安全上的权衡。随着技术的进步，专家们经常质疑最新系统是否实际上比旧系统风险更高。在1990年代末，Bishop撰写了一篇演讲，他认为计算机“远不如我们仍在使用且正被迅速取代的纸质系统安全”。从纸质向数字技术转变的担忧仍然普遍存在，尤其是在电子投票系统方面。一些人说电子投票机是可取的，部分原因是它们比纸质系统更快地产生选举结果。但这不足以说服其他人。“投票是我们民主的基石，”Hyppönen说。“这是我最不愿意以任何方式削弱的事情之一，尤其是当好处如此之小时。”军方也以不愿冒险而闻名。即使是世界上最活跃的军队，也因可靠性和安全性的原因，偶尔依赖旧技术。“我在乌克兰等地看到的一件事是使用纸质地图或塑封地图，以及指南针，”智库皇家联合军种研究所副研究员Thomas Withington说。“你无法干扰它。”他补充说，这是一种“模拟韧性”。Overlook Systems Technologies的系统工程师Victor Tasiemski表示，针对GPS导航的干扰攻击已迫使一些国家仔细选择保留哪些传统技术，以及投资哪些GPS替代方案。该公司从事导航技术工作。这正是爱尔兰发生的情况，那里更换地面无线电信标的计划被放缓，以延长这些信标的运行时间。爱尔兰航空管理局的一位女发言人6月告诉《爱尔兰时报》，保留这些信标是“计划中的韧性战略的一部分”。与军方合作的技术专家熟悉设计连接新旧技术的系统的挑战。Stefan Kraus是Kraus Hamdani Aerospace的联合创始人兼首席技术官，该公司设计了一个基于无人机的通信平台，可以将军事人员相互连接，无需

无论他们使用的是旧式电台还是新式电台，情况都是如此。他说，已有数十年历史的军用无线电技术“经过验证、测试且安全可靠”，“美国军方不会放弃这一技术。”  
勒索软件在我看来是过去10到15年间磁带得以存续的原因——  
雨果·梅拉特·塔西姆斯基指出，GPS导航的一种替代方案是eLoran，这是一种基于无线电的导航系统，其根源可追溯至二战期间首次开发的军事技术。塔西姆斯基表示，随着GPS系统遭受攻击，eLoran可以说正变得越来越受欢迎，因为它使用更强大的信号，因此更难被干扰：“要压制一个一兆瓦的发射机相当困难。”  
鲁棒性并非轻易能被替代。这一点同样适用于数据存储领域，在20世纪50年代发明的磁带至今仍扮演着重要角色。公司、研究机构和政府机构继续在磁带卷轴上存储大量数据。自问世以来，这项技术已显著改进，数据存储密度在几十年间呈指数级增长。但原理保持不变：承载信息的磁带卷轴。磁带可以脱离计算机系统，进行包装，并运输至安全设施，包括难以进入的地下洞穴和改造后的矿井。  
“勒索软件在我看来是过去10到15年间磁带得以存续的原因，”数据存储专业公司Quantum的首席执行官雨果·梅拉特表示。如果员工进行了良好的备份，例如使用磁带备份，那么一个被锁在自己计算机系统之外的组织仍可能检索到其最重要的数据。如今，对磁带的兴趣只会进一步增加，因为随机存取存储器（RAM）——一种不依赖磁带的计算机内存形式——的成本正在飙升。梅拉特表示，他公司的客户使用磁带存储各种数据——从广播公司拍摄的棒球比赛片段，到研究机构详细绘制的基因组图谱。  
更多类似内容：• 模拟技术可能令人沮丧——这是其吸引力的一部分吗？• 为什么模拟设计仍然经久不衰• 寻找旧电视的人们  
磁带的安全特性部分源于这样一个事实：大多数人往往根本不会与它互动。它是一种晦涩、笨重、老式的技术。“攻击系统的一种方法是布置一堆USB闪存盘，然后扔在停车场里，”毕晓普说，他指的是有人最终会捡起其中一个U盘并将其插入电脑的可能性——这是一种实施黑客攻击的简单方式。正如他所说：“你永远不会看到磁带被扔在停车场里。”接受BBC采访的专家仍然建议人们使用最新版本的磁带技术。

##段落

在日常任务中使用最新、最先进的技术仍然是最安全的方法。但值得承认的是，“新”并不一定在所有情况下都意味着“最好”。随着网络攻击和其他威胁变得越来越复杂，知道何时以及如何切换到较旧的系统可能会变得越来越重要。温宁顿再次提到乌克兰，俄罗斯在那里干扰了卫星通信，GPS导航也遭受了严重的信号干扰。没有哪个地方比这里更珍视“模拟韧性”了。温宁顿问道：“如果人们无法使用他们习以为常的技术，他们会怎么做？”——欲了解更多见解，请订阅我们的Tech Decoded新闻通讯，莉莉·贾马利和托马斯·杰曼将在其中解析科技界最重大的新闻，帮助你过上更好的数字生活。在此免费注册。欲了解更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境和健康报道，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。科技 计算机 犯罪 特写
